The Coast Guard has sent two vessels from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known as ​Port Blair, for ​the search-and-rescue operation, a Coast Guard spokesperson said.

World.title: Japan outlines measures to protect infrastructure from cyberattacks
World.content:
The government has drawn up draft guidelines outlining 150 measures that should be taken to enhance cybersecurity for businesses managing critical infrastructure.

The draft said that even closed networks disconnected from the internet “are not necessarily safe.” In light of a recent series of ransomware attacks, the draft urges such businesses to take measures, including taking out cybersecurity insurance.

The government will accept comments from the public on the guidelines until Wednesday. It plans to revise the draft based on feedback and release the final version by the end of September.

The government hopes that industry groups and government agencies will refer to the guidelines when developing safety standards.

The draft seeks action from businesses in 16 sectors, including finance, railways and electricity, designated as critical infrastructure.

Describing cybersecurity as “a management issue that can be key to the survival of a company,” the draft said that “it is difficult to completely protect against cyberattacks.”

Companies in the designated sectors are urged to improve their capabilities to recover from an attack, fully preparing for the possibility of system failures.

The draft cautioned against “overconfidence,” advising companies not to let their guard down because their systems use closed networks or dedicated operating systems or have unique technical specifications.

As recommended measures, the draft refers to taking out cybersecurity insurance to ease the possible massive financial impact caused by ransomware attacks, while asking companies not to pay ransoms.

To address cyberattacks utilizing advanced artificial intelligence models such as Claude Mythos, the draft mentions the need to strengthen defense measures promptly, including by using sophisticated AI models.

In view of progress in the development of quantum computers, the draft also calls for the adoption of postquantum cryptography, or PQC, which is hard to crack, by as early as 2035.

World.title: What a Tokyo summer taught this New Zealander about climate shock
World.content:
By the time I reached the middle of the sunflower field, my face had taken on an alarming shade of red.

The sunflowers I’d come to see in Kiyose, some towering as much as 2 meters above me, were magnificent. Distinctly less magnificent was the fact I’d inadvertently chosen to visit them on Tokyo’s hottest day of the year so far.

The mercury had climbed to 38 degrees Celsius. I was dripping with sweat, darting between islands of shade and clutching an increasingly futile handheld fan, wondering how I’d managed to overheat while doing little more than standing in a field and admiring the view.

Somehow, though, the people around me appeared to be having an entirely different experience.

An older woman ambled past in long trousers and sleeves that covered her wrists. Another couple posed for photos. An elderly gentleman tended to a vegetable patch nearby.

They weren’t exactly impervious to the heat — people clustered in the shade, covered up against the sun and waved electric fans in front of their faces — but nobody looked even remotely as close to melting as I felt.

I had lived in Tokyo as a child, at a time when I could spend summer days running around outside without giving much thought to the heat. But returning 25 years later, I was beginning to wonder whether Tokyo’s summers had changed — or I had.

As it turns out, both may be true.

According to Kazutaka Oka, head of the Climate Change Impacts Monitoring Research Section at the National Institute for Environmental Studies (NIES), Tokyo’s average temperature has risen by about 3 C over the past century.

One of those degrees can be attributed to climate change, with the other two linked to the urban heat island effect, he says.

Concrete and asphalt absorb the sun’s heat during the day and release it slowly, while buildings, traffic and air-conditioning systems pump more warmth into the surrounding air.

It’s an irony that isn’t lost on Oka. As temperatures rise, we retreat indoors and turn on the air conditioning, which in turn releases heat outside: “It’s a negative spiral,” he says.

Where once temperatures above 40 degrees were rare in Japan, they’re becoming increasingly common.

For Katie Ham, seeing Kiyose's magnificent sunflowers on Tokyo's hottest day of the year was a major dose of climate shock. | Ryan Anderson

So common, in fact, the Japan Meteorological Agency has even introduced the term kokushobi, or “cruelly hot day,” for days when the temperature exceeds 40 C.

It sounds almost comically dramatic, until you consider why a new phrase was needed in the first place. Suddenly, my sunflower-field meltdown seemed a little less like a personal failure.

But the problem with measuring heat solely by the temperature on the dial is that a single number rarely tells the whole story, Oka says.

Cue Tokyo’s characteristically high humidity, which seems to settle on your skin the moment you step outside and leaves you wondering whether you’ve accidentally been for a swim after walking for 10 minutes.

The humidity also makes it harder for sweat to evaporate, disabling one of the body’s key mechanisms for cooling itself, Oka says.

For someone arriving from a milder climate like me, that combination of heat and humidity can be particularly difficult to adjust to, he says.

The older you get, the harder it can be to acclimatize to as well. At the ripe age of 29, I can’t help but agree. It is, after all, the oldest I’ve ever been.

But instead of pretending the heat and humidity aren’t a problem, Japan has seemingly built an entire way of living around it.

Back home in New Zealand, surviving summer mostly means finding a beach, applying factor 50 sunscreen and praying for the best.

Here in Tokyo, an entire ecosystem has evolved around keeping cool. Portable fans hang from bags, parasols bloom along pavements and konbini become temporary refuges from the heat.

People take shelter from the sun in Tokyo's Shinjuku Gyoen on a hot summer's day. | Ryan Anderson

Armed with a basket and an open mind, I’ve raided Don Quijote to form my own personal arsenal, trying everything from cooling body wipes and frozen neck rings to UV parasols, portable electric fans, cooling sprays and every other gadget promising any semblance of relief.

Some products genuinely transformed my day-to-day life (God forbid I forget to charge my fan), while others have felt suspiciously close to expensive optimism.

But while today’s summer gadgets and gizmos might be more technically sophisticated, Japan actually has a long history of adapting to summer heat, according to Midori Nemoto, climate change adaptation coordinator at NIES.

Traditional adaptations included uchiwa (handheld fans), bamboo screens and uchimizu, or sprinkling water outside to cool the streets.

But it isn’t just about buying something to make the heat more comfortable, Nemoto says, it’s also about changing the way we live around it.

Human mobility data shows people reduce daytime outings as temperatures rise, shifting activities into the evening, she says.

“Sometimes adaptation is very simple: change the time, change the route, take a break, or even change your plans.” Learning the art of gradual acclimatization is important too, Nemoto says.

For example, before a big outdoor event, it can be useful to start getting your body used to the heat around two weeks in advance, perhaps even taking long hot baths to adjust.

That said, learning to adapt to the extreme heat shouldn’t mean just accepting it as the new norm, Nemoto warns.

“If extreme heat changes when people can safely work, travel, play outside or hold festivals, it could gradually change the way we live and experience the seasons in Japan,” she says. This year, Nemoto says she has been struck not only by the intensity of the heat but by how early the warmer days began and how long the heat can linger.

“We were already feeling very warm days quite early in spring, and the heat doesn’t necessarily end when the sun goes down either,” she says.

Midori Nemoto, climate change adaptation coordinator at the National Institute for Environmental Studies, says that before a big outdoor event, it can be useful to start getting your body used to the heat around two weeks in advance, perhaps even taking long hot baths to adjust. | Courtesy of Midori Nemoto

A longer hot season has its own risks — it can affect mental well-being as people stay indoors for longer periods of time, hamper food production, and disturb seasonal customs and traditions.

At its most devastating, the heat can even kill.

More than 1,500 people die from heatstroke in Japan each year — roughly 10 times the number of annual deaths from natural disasters such as earthquakes and typhoons.

Unlike an earthquake or typhoon, heatstroke rarely arrives as one singular event. Rather, it happens quietly, day after day, as people become accustomed to conditions that are actually very dangerous.

And then there’s the question of what happens in an even hotter world.

Oka expects Tokyo’s average temperature to continue rising, but says the increase in extreme temperatures may be more significant than the change in the average alone.

As was the case after the earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture last month, a heat wave combined with another natural disaster becomes significantly more dangerous due to power outages that reduce access to AC.

But it’s important not to write a Tokyo summer off quite yet.

From Nemoto’s perspective, it’s worth remembering that adaptation doesn’t have to be a grand, global undertaking.

It can begin much closer to home: in the buildings we live in, the way we move through our neighborhoods and the choices we make about how and when we spend time outside.

Perhaps that’s the lesson I’ve taken from my Tokyo summer too.

I arrived thinking I needed to find a way to beat the heat. Instead, I’ve learned to work around it — to seek shade, carry water, change my plans and, occasionally, admit defeat and retreat into the nearest air-conditioned shop.

It isn’t much in the face of a warming planet, but adaptation, Nemoto reminds me, has to start somewhere.

And besides, it would be a shame to give up on a Tokyo summer altogether. When the worst of the heat finally begins to loosen its grip, the city changes.

The lanterns come out, neighborhood festivals fill parks and temple grounds. Children emerge in yukata, food stalls pop up and Bon odori dancers circle beneath strings of lights as fireworks bloom above. It’s truly magical.

World.title: USA Fencing approaching run-up to LA Games as chance to take sport mainstream
World.content:
USA Fencing CEO Phil Andrews is betting the runup to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics can make the traditionally niche sport more widely popular in America, and is hoping that growth can reach beyond its affluent base.

A report by USA Fencing published this month shows its membership has reached an all-time high of 45,157, supported by a record 752 affiliated clubs across the country, which already surpasses the body’s original target of 700 expected by 2028.

The American fencing governing body is now targeting 70,000 members ahead of the Games, while its commercial push has also expanded, with marketing and communications projected to generate $2.8 million in the coming season.

World.title: South Korean survivor fights for workplace harassment ‘justice’
World.content:
Kept in the dark after reporting her boss for harassment, South Korean advocate Baek Song-yi is now campaigning for survivors’ right to know how their bullies were disciplined.

Baek, 40, experienced first-hand a troubling paradigm in South Korea’s workplace harassment response, with victims often expected to keep silent while employers have no clear legal duty to tell them how their cases ended.

At her former company, a U.S. firm with offices overseas, Baek said she was verbally harassed by her boss, an older man.

World.title: Nadeshiko Japan’s Saki Kumagai hoping to encourage more girls to play soccer
World.content:
Saki Kumagai, a defender for Nadeshiko Japan, is working to encourage more girls to play soccer while continuing her own career as an active player in England.

Through the general incorporated association Nadeshiko Care, or Nadecare, where she serves as representative director, Kumagai, 35, ran a program from March to April that sent elementary school girls on an overseas soccer trip.

“I want children to experience the world as early as possible,“ said Kumagai, who plays for the London City Lionesses in the Women’s Super League. “I want them to expand their own possibilities and options.”

World.title: Robots can outrun humans, but can they plug in a cable?
World.content:
China’s humanoid robots have shown they can run quicker than the fastest humans.

Now comes the real test: can they also handle packaging and warehouse operations while reliably performing precision tasks like connecting cables designed to evaluate their ability to work like humans in less flashy jobs?

The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games, which began Saturday in Beijing, combine events modeled on human sports with those designed to test the robots in simulated factories, restaurants, offices and in emergency situations.

World.title: Taiwan president touts peace through strength on China battle anniversary
World.content:
Peace can only be secured through strength and not even an inch of territory can be sacrificed, Taiwan President Lai Ching-te said on Sunday, visiting a sensitive front-line island to mark a key battle with Chinese forces almost seven decades ago.

Taiwan has controlled the Kinmen and Matsu islands, which lie just off the Chinese coast, since the Republic of China government fled to Taipei in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s communists. No peace treaty or armistice has ever been signed.

In heavy rain, Lai laid a wreath and bowed at a memorial park for the 68th anniversary of the 1958 clash with Chinese forces, known as the start of the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis — the last time Taiwanese and Chinese forces battled on a large scale.

Addressing veterans later, Lai expressed gratitude to those who “stood united and fought a bloody battle to repel communist totalitarian aggression.”

“Our resolve to unite in defending national sovereignty and safeguarding peace across the Taiwan Strait must never waver,” Lai said. “Peace has never simply fallen from the sky.”

The 1958 battle proves “that peace is secured through strength,” he said, adding it was necessary to maintain “the spirit of never yielding an inch” of Taiwan, Kinmen and another group of islands, while continuously boosting military spending.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has repeatedly denounced Lai as a “separatist.” He rejects Beijing’s sovereignty, saying only Taiwan’s people can decide their future, but has also offered talks with China.

Kinmen at its closest is less than 2 kilometers from Chinese-controlled territory. In the 1958 battle, Chinese forces began more than a month of bombardment of Kinmen, along with Matsu, including naval and air battles, seeking to force them into submission.

Taiwan fought back with support from the United States, though the crisis ended in a stalemate. Taiwan observes Aug. 23 every year as the date it fended off the Chinese attack.

China’s coast guard has since early 2024 conducted regular “law enforcement” patrols around Kinmen in Taiwan-controlled waters, to Taipei’s anger.

Referring to those patrols and other Chinese tactics, Lai said that for 68 years China had not stopped its “ambitions for external expansion for even a single day,” bringing “unease” across the Indo-Pacific.

Taiwan’s planned defense spending next year will exceed 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($30 billion) for the first time, the government announced on Thursday, and Lai said he hoped for strong support for the budget.

World.title: Painter supporting quake-hit Kumamoto with manga ‘Kinnikuman’
World.content:
A local painter is supporting reconstruction efforts in Kumamoto Prefecture, hit by a powerful earthquake last month, through collaborative works with the popular manga series “Kinnikuman.”

Kazuyuki Takishita, 50, was born in an area now in the Kumamoto town of Misato, where the July 28 quake recorded a seismic intensity of upper 6 on the shindo scale. He was working in his studio when the temblor struck.

The quake not only damaged his home and atelier but also toppled his stored works. More than 10 pieces were damaged, including those intended for exhibitions, and he had to dispose of some.

Despite this, he cleaned up his studio and resumed his activities about a week later.

Takishita is best known for his signature depictions of an ogre from the old Japanese folktale “Momotaro.” He took a liking to drawing in elementary school by reproducing pictures of Kinnikuman, the main character in the series, created by manga artist duo Yudetamago.

While supporting recovery efforts following the quake disaster that struck the same prefecture a decade ago, including by holding an exhibition in Tokyo, he became acquainted with Takashi Shimada, one half of Yudetamago. The two quickly got along.

In 2024, Takishita and the duo held a collaborative exhibition at Shimada’s suggestion.

In April this year, they held a reconstruction-themed exhibition related to the 2016 disaster in the city of Kumamoto. Part of the proceeds from collaboration works and goods, totaling ¥2.9 million, was donated to the city for repairs to Kumamoto Castle.

After the July quake, with Yudetamago’s consent, he drew Kinnikuman and an ogre from Momotaro propping up Kumamoto Castle together. Preparation is underway to sell this artwork on T-shirts and reusable shopping bags as charity items.

In September, Takishita plans to invite Shimada to Misato for an autograph session, in which Shimada will write the kanji character reading ”niku,” meaning meat, on the participants’ foreheads, imitating the main character Kinnikuman.

Born in the Kumamoto town of Chuo, which later became part of Misato, Takishita moved to Tokyo after graduating from high school. When Misato was established in 2004 through the merger of Chuo and another town, the municipality adopted the town emblem he designed. In 2022, he relocated back to his hometown.

Expressing his growing commitment to Misato, Takishita said, “I will continue to work hard to create works to help realize early reconstruction.”

World.title: 3 elderly people injured after escalator fall at Hong Kong shopping centre
World.content:
A 76-year-old man has been sent to hospital after falling on an escalator at a Hong Kong shopping centre, while two other elderly people sustained minor injuries, according to police.

The force received a report at 4.19pm on Sunday that three people had fallen on an escalator in phase one of Shek Lei Shopping Centre, leaving the man trapped.

He sustained injuries to his arms and legs and was taken to Princess Margaret Hospital.

Photos circulating online show fire services personnel and paramedics at the scene assisting the injured, with the escalator temporarily closed.

The same escalator was involved in a similar incident on August 1, when a 75-year-old woman carrying a one-year-old girl lost her balance and fell, landing on a 66-year-old woman and a 72-year-old man standing behind her.

All four sustained head injuries and abrasions to their limbs and were taken to the same hospital for treatment.

World.title: Divorcing devices: how digital detox helps Hongkongers ‘carve out moments’
World.content:
In the second instalment of a five-part Health Matters wellness series on Hong Kong’s growing wellness trends, Fiona Sun looks into how residents are embracing digital detox, as experts warn that excessive screen use is linked to anxiety, depression and sleep disorders.

For Robert Broad, stepping away from electronic devices has become part of a self-care routine he developed after the Covid-19 pandemic.

The 56-year-old recalled how spending long hours in front of screens while working remotely affected his physical and mental health and reduced the time he spent with family and friends.

“I became a lot more anxious, I wasn’t sleeping as much, I gained weight – all of those things started to snowball and take a toll on me and my relationships,” he said.

Determined to restore a sense of balance, Broad began with small, manageable steps that could develop into lasting habits.

When he returns home from work, he puts his mobile phone in a drawer. He has disabled news alerts and keeps notifications on only for his parents and anyone who may need to reach him in an emergency.

He has also switched his phone to greyscale to make it less appealing and checks his emails in batches rather than as they arrive. He stops checking them at 8.30pm each day.

World.title: ‘Huge influx’: expat retirees projected to drive Hong Kong’s premium home demand
World.content:
Hong Kong is tipped to see more luxury home sales with expatriates increasingly choosing the city as their retirement base, drawn to its low-tax environment as well as business opportunities, according to analysts.

“A huge influx of expats who used to live in Hong Kong are moving back with a long-term view to retirement,” said Victoria Allan, founder and CEO of Habitat Property.

“Many expats who previously would have left to retire are staying and purchasing [property] for the first time.”

A growing number of ultra-wealthy expatriates are choosing to remain in Hong Kong beyond their working years … rather than relocate elsewhere William Lau, Knight Frank

About 30 per cent of Habitat’s recent sales were contributed by expat clients, Allan said.

World.title: Chinese, Southeast Asian ride-hailing firms eye Hong Kong amid licensing roll-out
World.content:
More ride-hailing platform operators from mainland China and Southeast Asia have approached the Hong Kong government about entering the city’s market ahead of the launch of licensed operations, the transport minister has revealed.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also said on Sunday that more than 7,500 people had applied for the new combined taxi and ride-hailing vehicle written test, calling the number a “very good and positive” sign.

“We hope there will be more competition and greater diversity, which will provide more choices for residents and future ride-hailing drivers,” she said on a television programme.

Hong Kong legalised ride-hailing services earlier this year, requiring platforms, vehicles and drivers to obtain separate licences or permits.

Although the new regulatory regime took effect on August 3, the first licensed services are not expected to launch until later this year.

Chan said the operators included established companies that Hongkongers might have encountered while visiting the mainland or Southeast Asia, but she did not identify them or disclose how many had made contact.

World.title: Hong Kong to launch AI training for workers in November with big tech firms
World.content:
Hong Kong will partner with major technology firms to launch an AI training programme for the labour force in November as part of a government drive to equip workers with new skills, the city’s finance chief has said.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also said on Sunday the separate HK$50 million (US$6.4 million) “AI for All” push announced in February would feature more than 200 activities and was expected to benefit 50,000 people within two years.

Writing in his weekly blog, Chan noted the training programme would be carried out by the Employees Retraining Board

“The Employees Retraining Board will work with major tech enterprises to roll out AI courses in November to the employed population,” he said.

The board, which coordinates and funds market-oriented training courses, will be renamed Upskill Hong Kong as part of a revamp to promote continuous learning and skill improvement across the workforce.

“The development and application of frontier technology will pose challenges to the job market. We must speed up our response, helping young people master the skills and giving them opportunities to apply them in the workplace,” he said.

World.title: Untapped market: Hong Kong’s craft breweries push for permits to serve guests
World.content:
When a 100-member tour group from South Korea approached a Hong Kong craft beer manufacturer about a visit and tasting session, the operator declined their request.

The refusal was not due to a lack of confidence in the product or a staff shortage. The brewery simply lacked a licence to serve beer on the premises.

“It is not easy doing manufacturing in Hong Kong,” said Luke Yardley, founder of local craft beer brewery Yardley Brothers.

“It is just a missed opportunity when in every other country – if you are in London, New York, Dublin – customers can go for a day out and visit the brewery. They get to have a nice experience where they can consume alcohol on site. And the key thing is they can buy alcohol on site.”

Yardley is not alone. Many of Hong Kong’s craft beer manufacturers operate in industrial buildings under food factory licences to house their giant equipment and save costs, which makes applying for liquor licences difficult.

The situation has prompted calls for a review of the licensing regime governed by the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department to allow breweries to offer samples for walk-in customers, which industry leaders and a lawmaker have said could help support tourism.

World.title: Patient arrested after bedding, restraint belts set ablaze at Hong Kong hospital
World.content:
A patient has been arrested on suspicion of setting fire to bedding and restraint belts at a Hong Kong hospital, with no injuries reported.

Police arrested the 25-year-old man surnamed Wong at Kwong Wah Hospital in Yau Ma Tei for alleged arson. He remains in custody.

The fire was reported at 12.36am on Sunday after a security guard alerted police. The suspect allegedly set fire to bedding and restraint belts at the hospital.

Following a preliminary investigation, the Fire Services Department classified the blaze as suspicious, and police have taken over the case.

Arson carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment under Hong Kong law.

World.title: Hong Kong may issue typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as Narra approaches
World.content:
The Hong Kong Observatory may issue a typhoon signal on Tuesday or Wednesday as a tropical storm edges closer to the region.

“Tropical Cyclone Narra is expected to linger over the vicinity of Beibu Wan today and tomorrow, and then turn northeastwards gradually later on Monday to Tuesday, edging closer to the vicinity of Leizhou Peninsula,” the forecaster said on Sunday.

Leizhou Peninsula sits at the far southwestern tip of Guangdong province, some 400km (248.5 miles) west-southwest of Hong Kong.

“The Observatory will closely monitor its movement and the change in local wind conditions, and assess the need for issuing tropical cyclone warning signals on Tuesday or Wednesday,” it added, urging the public to pay attention to the latest weather information.

Narra is named after a tree species in the Philippines.

According to the forecast, there will be showers and squally thunderstorms early next week. The city’s temperatures will rise from 27 degrees Celsius (80.6 Fahrenheit) to 33 degrees on Friday.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.title: China Before the Infinite Camera Roll
World.content:
Of the many consumer goods that entered China in the 1980s, one small item transformed how millions of families recorded their lives: 35mm color negative film.

In 1984, Fujifilm established its Beijing office, as Chinese photographers were beginning to embrace the company’s color film, known for its green packaging and the distinctive greenish cast of its prints. Kodak, Fujifilm’s main rival at the time, soon followed, expanding its presence and introducing a network of express color photo stores across China in the 1990s.

These developments, together with the arrival of point-and-shoot cameras that required little skill to achieve proper exposure and sharp focus, enabled ordinary Chinese people to record their lives in color. The film was developed to produce negatives, which were then printed as photographs for family albums.

Not everyone kept the negatives. Many ended up at recycling plants, which is where French artist Thomas Sauvin’s work began. In 2009, Sauvin met Xiaoma, a Beijinger who recovered silver nitrate from X-rays, CDs, and negatives. The two struck a deal, and Sauvin received his first batch of negatives to digitize. Their partnership would eventually help create one of China’s largest private archives of photographic negatives: the Beijing Silvermine.

The project gives broader significance in banal, amateur images. As patterns emerge across dozens, sometimes hundreds, of photographs, personal moments become part of a collective record. One example is a series of portraits taken beside refrigerators, an appliance many Chinese households were acquiring for the first time in the 1990s. Together, such images document the transformation of everyday life as a rapidly changing China became wealthier and more urban.

Much has changed since then. Film gave way to digital cameras, and then to smartphones. People can now easily take thousands of photos a year, a number unthinkable to most families in the 1990s, when a roll of film contained just 36 exposures.

More recently, however, analog photography has enjoyed a revival on social media, where users are drawn to its vintage tones and textures. In 2025, Lucky Film, a Chinese manufacturer that once competed with Kodak and Fujifilm, announced the return of its color negative film amid growing demand from nostalgic millennials and curious Gen Z consumers. Yet a roll of film and lab processing now cost more than 100 yuan (US$14.80) for just 36 photos, leaving analog photography a niche hobby.

The intention behind analog photography has also changed, according to Sauvin. “Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative, and they will post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram,” said Sauvin, who does not shoot film himself.

What has been lost? Humor, perhaps. Looking through the Beijing Silvermine images, it is hard not to be struck by the ease with which people posed and smiled, gazing into the camera with little of the self-consciousness or affectation common in photography today. Before social media, people seemed simply to be enjoying the moments they were living.

In June, Sixth Tone sat down with Sauvin to discuss what analog photography reveals about the lives of ordinary Chinese people in the 1990s and today, his own relationship with the archive, and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence. The interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Sixth Tone: What was your first impression of the earliest batches of recycled negatives, and how did you begin to interpret their meaning?

Sauvin: They were very banal. Quite boring, sometimes very repetitive. It took maybe two or three years before I started to understand what I could do with them. At some point, because of the quantity, you leave the universe of personal stories and enter the universe of collective memory.

A simple example is that, at the beginning of the project, I came across a photo of a woman posing next to a fridge. And I thought, “Oh, having your portrait taken with a fridge is an unusual thing to do.” Then I saw another one, then another one, and now I probably have a series of 25 pictures like this. In the early 1990s, households in Beijing began acquiring refrigerators. They would decorate them and take photos with them. And that’s something no one else would really record. A photojournalist would never make a series about this, nor would a historian or an artist. It’s too close to daily life. It’s too simple. Yet ordinary people, accidentally and unconsciously, capture the bigger picture in these negatives.

Sixth Tone: Is there a single frame or series that interests you most?

Sauvin: So many. I like the photos taken at Beijing World Park. It opened in 1993, and people went there to get a sense of travel, to experience the outside world and its monuments. In the archive, I have thousands of photos taken there in 1993, 1994, and 1995. It was the perfect playground for taking photos. You could have your picture taken with the Twin Towers, the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower, and so on.

Then, when I went through photos taken in the early 2000s, these Chinese tourists weren’t at the World Park anymore. They were in the actual countries. And when I look at these negatives, as a French person, I always wonder: Is it the real one or the World Park one?

Sixth Tone: Besides the Eiffel Tower series, were there any photos that connected the collection to your own life?

Sauvin: A lot. I was born and raised in Paris, so I’m attentive to photos taken there. I found photos taken on Rue Fabert in the 7th arrondissement, where I learned to walk when I was 1 year old. It’s my home. Seeing someone posing right where I learned to walk was a strange feeling.

I also remember going to the Louvre Museum as a kid and seeing tourists taking photos: flash, flash, flash! Two or three decades later, I started the Silvermine project and found those kinds of photos. Because they were photographing oil paintings with a flash, you always get this big white dot in the image. I made a series about them called “Dazzling Old Masters.”

But the entire archive also has a very strong connection with me. The first time I went to Beijing was in 1999, on a family exchange. In 2009, exactly 10 years later, I started this project, which allowed me to discover the Beijing that existed before I arrived. I wouldn’t have done that with any other city in the world.

Sixth Tone: Have you been able to contact the people in these images?

Sauvin: There’s a photo I found in 2010 that I absolutely love: a young girl posing on a red motorcycle on a street in Dashilar, Beijing. One day, she got in touch with me on Weibo and said, “That girl on the bike, it’s me.” She sent me the printed photo from her family album.

I immediately sent her the other 35 photos from the same roll, and she discovered many that she’d probably never seen because people didn’t always print every photo. Looking through them, she realized that the roll contained four consecutive birthdays, meaning the film had been in the family camera for more than four years. They had to wait that long to finish the roll, have it developed, and finally see the images.

That says a lot about how our relationship with photography has changed and how analog photography captures who we are as human beings in a very pure way. Because it costs money and takes time, you make sure to record the moments that matter. I really like the idea of these latent images sitting in a film canister for four years, then one day being put into chemicals and revealing all these moments. And I find it crazy that, after waiting four years, the negatives could be thrown away the very next day.

Sixth Tone: There is a fine line between the privacy of these images and the public nature of your collection and exhibitions. How do you navigate that tension?

Sauvin: Of course, I’m dealing with very private, intimate photos that were never meant to be used in a book or shown in an exhibition. People are vulnerable because they are themselves. That’s something I always try to keep in mind.

I always make sure not to make fun of people. That’s not easy, because a very important part of the Beijing Silvermine’s visual universe is its sense of humor. There’s something very light, funny, and fresh about it. So you need to preserve that sense of humor because it’s the soul of the project, while never crossing the line into making fun of people.

Another rule I’ve given myself almost since the beginning is that I generally avoid using two images of the same person. That way, I make sure never to delve too deeply into one person’s life. What brings the photos together are more anthropological themes. The photos come together and contribute to a theme. But I would not be comfortable showing many photos taken by the same person.

In 2015, a very good friend of mine in Beijing came to me with a big cardboard box containing all the negatives and photos of her late father. He took a lot of photos and organized everything very neatly, with handwritten information everywhere: Here are the 120 films; there are the 35mm films. It was absolutely beautiful.

She gave it to me and said, “I think you’re doing great things with negatives, so this is yours, and just do what you want with it.” I was never able to open the box a second time because it was not my place to deal with this material. It all comes from one person. I know who this person is, so I can do absolutely nothing with it.

Sixth Tone: How do your curatorial decisions reflect the way you view analog photographs within their historical context?

Sauvin: In this exhibition, curated by Holly Russell at Fotografiska Shanghai, we present one room with 1,300 prints. That’s the selection I’ve been working on for 16 years. The selection was organized around themes, topics, and angles that emerged organically from the archive.

But when we brought the archive to Shanghai, we decided not to present each series together. Everything is mixed, so it’s up to the viewer to look at the photos and, just like I did, start seeing connections between them. I also didn’t decide which photo would go where. They were hung quite randomly by the workers who installed the show, and some amazing connections happened simply because of that.

We also decided to present everything as 10-by-15-centimeter prints, which is probably the size of the prints that would have been made from these negatives for family albums. No photo is bigger than another, so we’re not claiming that one is more important. What makes them powerful is their coming together.

There’s something about found photography, about vernacular photography, that is completely crazy: Quantity is more important than quality. You need quantity to make the switch from personal memory to collective memory. That’s how you end up with a gigantic photo album. It’s not the album of a family. It’s the album of a city, a generation, a place, and a time.

Sixth Tone: We have seen a resurgence of analog photography recently, globally but especially in China. Lucky Film is producing color negative film again. What do you make of this renewed interest? Why do you think it appeals to young Chinese people?

Sauvin: I suppose it’s about our relationship with the medium. We’re always drawn to technologies from the past. We’ve seen this with music. We had vinyl records, then CDs, MiniDiscs, and MP3s, and now we are going back to vinyl. There is a worldwide trend of people going back to analog photography. I’m not sure I’m very interested in that. Now we’re at a stage where we’re mass-producing images, and I’d rather live in my time and do that than go back to an earlier, previous tool.

And there’s something very different. People 30 years ago were shooting analog, but there was no artistic intention or intention to share these photos online. There wasn’t this element of staging or representation.

Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative and post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram. So the intention is not pure. In the end, what does it mean? It means it’s a filter, like a vintage filter of some kind. That’s why I’m not very interested in the trend. I love analog photography, but it died about 20 years ago.

Sixth Tone: Artificial intelligence is being used to restore and recreate faded or damaged negatives. Do you see it primarily as a boon or a bane?

Sauvin: I find it completely fascinating, and I’m sure that, combined with the right idea, it could be an amazing tool. I’m really open to it.

That being said, I need to be very careful because I have this Silvermine archive of 1 million photos, all made of flesh and blood, that come from ordinary people. They are physical objects, and for so many years, when I scanned a photo and shared it, people trusted that the photo existed. There was no question about that.

Then suddenly, about a year ago, we had this explosion of AI-generated images, and it changed people’s minds, mine as well. Now when you see a photo, the first question you ask yourself is: Is it real, or is it AI?

I really don’t want that confusion to happen with the Silvermine. I want to make it very clear: I deal only with analog photography, and I do not modify the photos in any way.

World.title: China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018923/China’s First Booster Landing Marks Leap Toward Reusable Rockets
World.content:
China has landed an orbital rocket’s booster, rather than discarding it, for the first time, paving the way for sustainable rocket launches and potentially cutting future launches’ costs by tens of millions of yuan.

The Aug. 19 milestone by Chinese aerospace startup LandSpace also makes China the second country after the U.S. to successfully recover rocket boosters on both solid ground and at sea — the latter feat accomplished last month.

U.S.-based aerospace companies SpaceX and Blue Origin were previously the only enterprises to have successfully landed rocket boosters on solid ground. SpaceX has also recovered boosters at sea — by landing them vertically on drone ships — compared with China’s net-capture method.

On Wednesday at 7:35 am, the 66.1-meter-tall Zhuque-3 lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Pilot Zone in the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, and delivered an internet satellite into its designated orbit.

The rocket’s stainless-steel booster, carrying nine liquid oxygen-methane engines, later landed 390 kilometers away in neighboring Gansu province.

A similar attempt by the same company on Dec. 3 last year failed following combustion. On the latest model, the team improved the landing propulsion system and added protective structures, domestic media reported.

China’s push to build extensive low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks — “megaconstellations” of coordinated satellites operating 2,000 kilometers or less above Earth — is driving growing demand for cheaper, more frequent rocket launches.

Such networks aim to provide services such as high-speed internet access in remote areas. The country currently has a few hundred satellites in orbit, and tens of thousands are ultimately planned.

A rocket’s booster, located at the bottom of the ship and used in the initial stage of launch, is commonly the most expensive component, accounting for 70% or more of a rocket’s hardware costs, LandSpace told domestic media. Traditionally, however, they are discarded after launch, leaving the upper part of the rocket to continue toward orbit.

Reuse of a common nine-engine booster could save at least 20 million to 50 million yuan ($2.9 million to $7.4 million), Zhang Liang, technical lead of a reusable rocket research team at Sun Yat-sen University’s School of Aeronautics and Astronautics, told domestic media.

However, Zhang added that China still faces a shortage of launch facilities. The cost advantage of reusable rockets will only become significant if there are enough launches for rockets to be reused multiple times a year.

According to LandSpace, the cost per launch could fall by about 45% after five uses. The Zhuque-3’s first stage is designed to be reused at least 20 times, with the company ultimately aiming to bring launch costs below 20,000 yuan per kilogram of payload.

LandSpace told domestic media that it plans to relaunch the recovered booster as soon as possible.

Over the past decade, supportive policies from the central government have led more private companies to enter China’s space sector, which state-owned enterprises previously dominated.

Last November, the China National Space Administration released a two-year action plan pledging to expand access to rocket testing facilities and strengthen international cooperation. The space sector is also listed as a strategic priority in China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, which began this year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 rocket booster lands in Minqin, Gansu province, Aug. 19, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.content:
Chinese supermarket chain Pangdonglai has announced the recruitment of former convicts for the second year in a row, expanding its hiring scope to employees who have spent at least five years in prison. The move has sparked renewed debate over the line between reducing employment discrimination against former inmates and upholding public safety.

The plan, announced Aug. 14 by the company’s branch in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, involves recruiting 20 people who have served sentences of at least five years. The store is set to open in October.

Pangdonglai was founded by Yu Donglai in 1995. Based in Henan’s Xuchang City, it has gained a reputation for offering relatively high pay, shorter working hours, and generous time off — emphasizing employee well-being over profit.

Employees work no more than 36 hours per week — in China, the legal limit is 40 hours — and receive 40 days of paid leave annually, including 10 “mental health” days. In the first quarter of 2026, employees’ average monthly salary was 9,600 yuan ($1,400), compared with roughly 5,800 yuan at China’s private wholesale and retail businesses.

Last year, the company recruited former convicts for the first time. Applicants were required to have served no more than 10 years in prison, be under the age of 35, and have a middle school education or higher.

Yu said in a Saturday post on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, that all 30 former convicts hired last year remain employed by the company.

This year, the company looks to recruit former inmates who have served sentences of at least five years.

The move quickly divided opinion online. Supporters praised the company for giving convicts a second chance. Lin Minming, founder of Red Apple Public Welfare, an organization that supports the children of prisoners, told domestic media that the company’s decision to continue hiring ex-convicts, particularly those who “may be facing even more difficult employment challenges,” is “worth paying attention to.”

“In the past, people would make baseless assumptions when talking about this issue — worrying that former inmates would be difficult to manage, unstable, or likely to cause problems,” Lin said. “Now that there’s at least a group of real (ex-convicts) working in a real company, we can see what happens.”

Former inmates in China face significant barriers to finding jobs. Fewer than 40% secure employment because of their criminal records, according to local media.

But others raised concerns. “Many people serving more than five years (in prison) were convicted of serious crimes,” one user wrote online. “Supermarkets are crowded places frequented by ordinary people, including children and the elderly. People who have turned their lives around deserve a second chance, but customer safety should not be overlooked.”

Others argued that giving special opportunities to former inmates is unfair to those who have always obeyed the law.

Responding to the concerns, the company told domestic media that people convicted of sexual or violent offenses are ineligible, and that applicants with nonviolent offenses will be prioritized. It added that those hired will initially be assigned to back-office positions such as warehousing and logistics, rather than customer-facing jobs, and undergo a six-month trial period.

China has been strengthening support for former inmates returning to society. A revised Prison Law, passed in April and set to take effect this November, states that discriminating against former convicts in employment, education, or social security matters is illegal.

Former inmates will also be required to undergo “pre-release education” — including legal and psychological counseling, vocational training, and daily-life skills — encouraging them to pursue employment and entrepreneurship.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Customers crowd a Pangdonglai supermarket in Xuchang, Henan province, May 1, 2026. VCG)
