World.title: Police search for missing man in High Country
World.content:
Police are searching for an 85-year-old man who went missing from Harrietville in Victoria's north-east last on Sunday night.

Jacobus, also known as John, was last seen leaving the Harrietville Hotel shortly after 10pm.

John, whose last name has not been released, had been at the hotel with his wife.

The pair have a regular routine where she walks the 200 metres south along the Great Alpine Road to home while he drives.

John was driving the couple's silver 2007 Toyota LandCruiser, registration WBD-077, but when his wife arrived home, John and the car were not there.

John's family and friends are searching Harrietville and surrounding areas. (Supplied: Colin Finnie)

Police and family members are concerned for John's welfare as he does not usually travel far by himself and was expected to go directly home.

Search continues

Local police have searched around Harrietville and Bright, including local tracks.

The Police Air Wing has also searched around Mount Hotham and along the Great Alpine Road, while friends of John have also joined the search.

Harrietville is a small town in the Alpine National Park, north-east of Melbourne. (Google Maps)

Police have released an image of John, who is described as Caucasian, with a slim build and about 170 centimetres tall.

He walks hunched over and uses a walking stick, and is unable to walk long distances.

He was last seen wearing a checked shirt, a vest and pants, and may have been wearing a hat.

His Toyota LandCruiser has a font nudge bar and two spotlights.

Police have asked anyone who has seen John or his car to contact Triple Zero (000).

World.title: Mundi Mundi Bash still ultimate outback adventure, festival goers say
World.content:
For many, the Mundi Mundi Bash music festival is the ultimate adventure: a road trip to an isolated outback venue for music and fun.

Held 38 kilometres north-west of Broken Hill, the far-flung festival was preparing for its fifth bash with headline acts including The Teskey Brothers, John Butler and Jessica Mauboy when disaster struck.

An unseasonably heavy amount of rain partially flooded 30 per cent of the festival grounds and, on the day music goers should have been rolling in, organisers had to make the "gut-wrenching" decision to turn away 5,000 ticketholders.

Record rainfall led to the campground being partially flooded. (Supplied: Sharyn Cunningham)

Event organiser Laura Impey said she and her father Greg Donovan, who founded the festival, were "shattered" they had to turn so many people away.

"We don't take it lightly, the journey and the effort people put in to get here, so to have to make this call is beyond devastating," she said.

Graham Tainton, from Melbourne, was one of the displaced travellers and had been "really looking forward" to his first bash, but understood why the decision had to be made.

"We can't help what Mother Nature is going to do," he said.

Cheryl and Murrary Simpson, Jenny McFarland and Elizabeth Bate were some of the displaced ticketholders. (ABC Broken Hill: Soofia Tariq)

Jenny McFarland was also turned away after a 12-hour drive, but she and her friends decided to make the best of their time in Broken Hill, where some of the Bash acts put on free concerts.

"This was going to be my first Mundi, but we'll come back another year," Ms McFarland said.

Sharyn Cunningham says the event was different this year due to the rain and the cost-of-living pressures. (Supplied: Sharyn Cunningham)

Fourth-year basher Sharyn Cunningham from the Barossa Valley, South Australia, was able to get into the festival after initially being turned away.

She said the rain and cost-of-living was having an obvious impact on attendees.

"I've noticed a difference. People are not using many vendors as much as normal. I think everyone is doing it a little bit tougher, I can see that and also with the humungous puddles out front," she said.

"I think people are just staying in the caravans a bit more. Not as many people [are] going to the concert."

Outback music festival defies trends

The Mundi Mundi Bash has steadily grown from its first year in 2022 with about 9,500 attendees to 15,000 at this year's sold-out festival.

The outback event is one of only a few festivals still thriving in Australia, as many others were scaled back and even cancelled entirely due to soaring overhead and production costs as well as cost-of-living pressures driving a downturn in ticket sales.

Last month Mundi's sister festival, the Big Red Bash, had to be cancelled.

The wet weather could not dampen spirits among the 10,000 ticketholders who were able to get access to event after heavy rain. (Supplied: Mundi Mundi Bash)

While the decision was largely due to flooding of the Birdsville site, uncertainty about fuel prices and availability had also played a part.

Ahead of the Mundi Bash, returning "bashers" Natelie and Wayne Chambellant, from Tamworth, said the fuel crisis had been a challenge.

"We both discussed that when the fuel prices were rising and we basically decided it didn't matter how high they rose, it was the availability of the fuel, we were coming regardless," Ms Chambellant said.

Natelie and Wayne Chambellant say the friendly atmosphere of the Bash made them return despite higher fuel costs. (ABC Broken Hill: Soofia Tariq)

Mundi founder Greg Donovan said the event's uniqueness helped it survive when so many other festivals and events struggled.

"It's a different style of music festival. People are not just coming for the music, obviously the music is a major drawcard, but it's the location, it's the setting, it's the vibe … it's just a sense of community," he said.

Greg Donovan says the event offers a unique experience. (Australian Story: Erin Semmler)

He said people were drawn to the road tripping and camping at a remote outback venue.

"The combination of all of that is really what sets it apart and is what is making it successful and sustainable."

In the lead-up to the festival, Mr Donovan said fuel prices were not a major obstacle for many of the bashers, as they tended to plan ahead.

"They come out to usually do a two-week trip and have a holiday and have a great time," he said.

"And if they might have to pay an extra couple hundred bucks all up for their fuel, it's something they will just generally absorb."

Glenn and Dianne Carlos, and their dog Whisky, are making the most of their "bucket-list" trip to the Mundi Mundi Bash. (ABC Broken Hill: Soofia Tariq)

This was the case for Glenn and Dianne Carlos, from Canberra, who said the Mundi Mundi Bash had been on their bucket list for a long time.

"Fuel prices are an issue and we're not underplaying the issue of what fuel prices are, but if you make a decision to come out here, whether it's 10 or 20 cents extra a litre really isn't that big a deal," Mr Carlos said.

For the Canberrans, the Bash offered a priceless experience of being in the "middle of nowhere with no power" with "great music".

Caravanning a 'cost-effective' way to travel

Andrea and Gus Wegener from Mannum, South Australia, had been waiting five years to use their 2021 Bash tickets.

The festival's first-ever year was postponed due to the COVID pandemic and it was not until 2026 that they could make the trip.

Ms Wegener said while the cost of fuel was high, caravanning at the festival had allowed them to keep costs down.

"It is good that you can bring all your own gear … even though we plan on buying some food and supporting the stalls," she said

Andrea and Gus Wegener (second and third from left) with friends Mandy and Sid Underwood and Loris and Sparky Dabinett getting ready for Mundi Mundi. (ABC Broken Hill: Soofia Tariq)

"It definitely does make it a lot more cost efficient, once you've paid for your fuel you can counteract that [because] you don't have to pay for accommodation."

First-timers Mel and Dan Miegel from Avalon Beach in Sydney saw the Bash online and decided it would be the perfect trip in their new caravan.

"We do appreciate it's a real pinch at the moment for everybody, including us," Ms Miegel said.

Dan and Mel Miegel took their new van on the road to the Mundi Mundi Bash. (ABC Broken Hill: Soofia Tariq)

"We're fortunate with the van, having that allows us to cook a lot of our own meals, keeps the accommodation cost low and then we can do some free camping on our way here and back," Mr Miegel said.

Being able to bring her beloved dogs to the festival was also a huge drawcard.

"They are my best friends and I think it's amazing that we can bring our dogs," Ms Miegel said.

World.title: The 'heartfelt' spaces drawing crowds away from traditional music venues
World.content:
Craig Pieterson has been welcoming nearly 70 musicians a week into his Marrickville venue Lazybones Lounge for more than 13 years.

But with dwindling alcohol sales and rising costs, the model his cosy music bar is built on is not working like it used to.

"Everyone's doing it tough. I make more money on the door occasionally than I do over the bar and we've never seen that," Mr Pieterson said.

He said while audiences were still engaging with music, without bar spend to offset costs, the numbers did not add up.

"It's the bills that kills it," he said.

Alcohol sales are down at Craig Pieterson's Lazy Bones Lounge. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

Mr Pieterson is one of 33 recipients of a third round of New South Wales government grants aimed at propping up struggling venues following a spate of recent closures, including the nearby Moshpit Bar, Lazy Thinking and Mary's Underground.

"We're investing in the core music venues, venues that are playing five or six nights a week," Music and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham said.

"They're the ones employing musicians."

The venues, located across the state, will receive a share of $3.8 million for upgrades like soundproofing, new equipment, lighting and LED screens.

Focusing on screen and lighting, the government said, would help venues provide "compelling audiovisual experiences" to counter the competition from streaming, social media and other new media.

"For me to be better at providing a product that is of high-end world class, that's the only way I'd be able to achieve it," Mr Pieterson said.

Lazy Bones in Marrickvile is among 33 venues across NSW getting a cash injection. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

Growth of 'DIY' shows

But while traditional venues have been fighting to keep the lights on, bands performing in skate parks, backyards, warehouses and boxing gyms have been attracting enviable crowds.

The so-called "DIY" shows require a space and audience, and everything else is left up to the creativity of organisers.

They may or may not be ticketed, are often advertised through word of mouth or social media, and usually do not serve alcohol.

Warehouses are among the venues hosting DIY music events. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

At a DIY event in Marrickville, musicians performed in a boxing ring, and at another in Sydenham, the audience sat on the edges of a skate park while bands played inside the bowl.

At one event over the weekend, people danced around a giant egg in an Eveleigh warehouse.

One of the organisers, artist EJ Son, said the idea was born out of a chance meeting with fellow organiser and musician Grace Barr at an Ashfield sauna.

The pair spent two weeks recruiting other artists and musicians to help, borrowing sound equipment from friends, designing a line-up and installing two key artworks in the room.

"When it's just DIY with artists, there's a bit of an understanding of the need to be spontaneous and it's really special," EJ Son said.

Bands have been performing in boxing rings. (Supplied: Felix El James)

They have access to the space through an artist residency that is coming to an end, and while they were not exactly advertising the gig to owners, the potential for something "cool" was too tempting.

"I've got nothing to lose and it just needs to happen," they said.

Barr, who is a banjo player and singer, said getting consistent gigs had been difficult in Sydney.

"I think it is getting harder to find regular shows with venues that are able to offer a fee," Barr said.

While DIY gigs generally do not pay musicians, Barr said it was a chance to play in a less structured way instead of regimented sets.

"Maybe I want to experiment with playing for 30 minutes and then having a pause, and then someone's going to do a tap dance or someone's going to do a tap dance," the musician said.

"Which I think curators are interested in, but you don't have to ask for permission with a DIY show."

DIY shows offer musicians a less structured way to play. (Supplied: Felix El James)

Changing needs of audiences

Joe Hardy has been paying close attention to the DIY scene as part of his work as the co-founder of popular gig-guide SydneyMusic.Net.

He attributes much of the success of DIY shows to their creativity and sense of community.

"I think DIY is a lot more open-ended, and probably a lot more open-hearted as well, and I think that's what people are responding to and why the audiences are building at such a rate," Mr Hardy said.

Special entertainment precincts expand Taran Howard opened up his small bar in Sydney's inner west last September. Since then, he has learnt how to mix drinks "on the fly".

He said amid prolonged challenging conditions for venue owners, many have failed to remain attentive to changing audience sentiment.

"People talk a lot about reduction in drinking, but I actually think it's more nuanced and complex than that.

"People have different ideas around what they want to feel in terms of belonging in a space."

That can boil down to simple decisions like where people will sit and stand, where performers are positioned in a room, what hospitality is offered to attendees and how long people are invited to stay after the music ends.

"The number of occasions where we see people really doing very heartfelt and very accommodating, and warm hosting of people in their spaces, and that really changes the dynamics."

World.title: Live: ASX set to lift as Wall Street slump arrested
World.content:
The ASX is poised to rise this morning after Wall Street regained some momentum in a jittery week's trading.

When futures trading closed on Saturday morning, the ASX 200 was priced to rise about 0.5%, which would claw back a large chunk of the 0.6% it shed last week.

The three key Wall Street indices made gains.

S & P 500: +0.4%

+0.4% Dow: +1.0%

+1.0% Nasdaq: +0.4%

However, over the week, the benchmark S & P 500 fell 1.4%.

The tech-centric Nasdaq's rise ended a five-day losing streak.

All week, equity market investors had been taking their cues from the direction of US government bond yields as the prospect of higher borrowing costs dampened risk appetite.

Nerves were looking increasingly frayed as 30-year Treasury Bond yields hit almost 20-year highs.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent attempted to calm markets, saying that the government could further increase its Treasury repurchases after a surprise announcement on Wednesday that it would spend double the expected amount on bond buybacks.

Northlight Asset Management chief investment officer Chris Zaccarelli told Reuters that after a seesaw trading week, Friday seemed calmer on Wall Street.

"In the middle of the week, equity investors were concerned yields could be on a one-way trip higher," Chris Zaccarelli said. "With the Treasury Department announcement, investors aren't as worried anymore."

So far, the US Treasury's actions have done little to suppress rising interest rates but have done a decent job of undermining the US dollar against most major currencies.

The Aussie dollar closed higher last week at 71.74 US cents, its highest weekly close in three months.

The US dollar upheaval also saw gold hit a three-month high, climbing above the $US4,600/ounce mark for the first time since May.

There was at least a bit of comforting news on the US economic front helping to ease investor worries, with data showing the strongest growth in the US services sector in nearly two years powered a sharp acceleration in overall business activity in August.

However, this was offset by a slowing of growth in a manufacturing sector that is being restrained by reduced stock building and supply disruptions from the Iran war.

Earlier, UBS Global Wealth Management raised its year-end target for the S & P 500 to 8,100, citing a stronger earnings outlook and robust corporate profit growth.

Adding to inflation concerns, however, oil futures settled higher for a sixth straight day, after US President Donald Trump threatened economic sanctions on Iran's trading partners, raising expectations of tighter supply.

Iran shot back with threats of a "devastating" response to any US actions, as disruptions continue to hamper oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Seven commodity ships sailed along the Strait on Thursday, which was only half the previous day's tally, data from ship-tracker Kpler showed.

For the week, Brent futures gained 6.4% while US West Texas Intermediate futures rose 5.7%.

With Reuters

World.title: Sydney councillor laments 'huge failure' amid short-term rental boom
World.content:
As Sydney grapples with rising homelessness and low vacancy, local councils hold little power to act against short-term accommodation operators some say are draining the city's long-term rental supply.

Homelessness NSW has called for a 7.5 per cent levy on providers who rent out their properties on platforms such as Airbnb and Stayz, arguing it could generate millions to fund housing support services and free up extra rental stock.

In Sydney, where the vacancy rate sits at 2.1 per cent, there were 10,531 active listings for Airbnbs alone in August, according to market analysis from AirRoi.

City of Sydney Deputy Lord Mayor Jess Miller has supported the push for a crackdown on Airbnbs, but said limited data available to councils made it difficult to identify which were homes being lived in or investment properties being used solely for short-term accommodation.

Jess Miller is concerned short-stay investors could buy up new residential apartment blocks without stronger regulation. (ABC News: Nandini Dhir)

Cr Miller said with thousands of new dwellings flagged under the housing delivery authority, there was nothing preventing investors from exploiting new residential developments "to in effect rezone them to commercial, by solely using them as accommodation properties".

"The mythology of the solution to the problem is more supply is completely eroded when you look at what the supply that we have is actually being used for," she said.

In 2021, the state government introduced a 180 day cap on short-term rentals where hosts do not occupy the entire home, and required all properties in the sector to be registered to track compliance breaches.

There are more than 10,000 Airbnbs in Sydney, according to market analysis. (ABC News: Millie Roberts)

But Cr Miller said because information on the short-term rental accommodation (STRA) database was only accessible by the state government, local councils had limited enforcement capability.

"The government needs to be able to provide us a database that is completely transparent, that identifies properties, their ownership status, their use status, the nights that they are being rented out on and the revenue being generated," she said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure told the ABC that councils were responsible for enforcing planning laws relating to individual properties, including short-term accommodation rentals.

The spokesperson said the department provided quarterly data from the NSW STRA register to Airbnb at its request to understand how short-term rental activity was changing across council areas over time.

At this stage, no other booking platforms had made requests for this data, the spokesperson added.

Sydney is grappling with rising homelessness and low vacancy. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Council investigates ban

The City of Sydney is currently considering a ban on short-term rental accommodation in areas where concentration is high, or where vacancy rates fall below three per cent.

The Greens-led proposal estimated the move could return up to 5,000 properties to the long-term rental market.

Greens Councillor Sylvie Ellsmore said in Millers Point, where public housing was sold off by the former Coalition government, the situation was "particularly grotesque".

"Most of those homes used to be public housing, [they] used to be where low-income people could live," she said.

"Now they are Airbnbs … which represents a huge failure of government policy."

Sylvie Ellsmore reflected on the rise of short-stay rentals in Millers Point. (Supplied)

The Greens believe the proposal could return up to 5,000 properties to the long-term rental. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

Cr Ellsmore said the impact of Airbnbs in the area had led to the closure of a historic childcare centre due to dwindling enrolments, and believed no fines had ever been issued for enforcement breaches.

"Councils want to do things that their community needs, but we're very restricted under the current laws unless the state government changes them," she said.

A spokesperson for Airbnb ANZ told the ABC the vast majority of its listed properties were primary residences and homes used periodically by their owners.

An Airbnb spokesperson says the majority of its listed properties are primary residences used periodically by owners. (Flickr)

The spokesperson said Airbnb remained committed to being a constructive partner to the City of Sydney during its proposal but added, "successful policy must target chronic undersupply, which is the primary driver of the housing crisis".

Stayz senior director of government and corporate affairs, Eacham Curry, said the company supported "fit-for-purpose regulation" of the STRA sector.

Mr Curry said any levy introduced should be of "a reasonable level" and "applied uniformly to all short-term accommodation providers".

Local councils hold limited enforcement capability to act against short-stay accommodation investors who break the rules. (ABC News: Miriah Davis)

Delays to short-term rental accommodation review

Both Cr Ellsmore and Cr Miller queried the release of the government's review into STRA, which they described as "massively overdue" and potentially "outdated".

Premier Chris Minns vowed to crack down on the issue amid the housing crisis, with a review into the STRA sector announced in 2024.

"We don't know if it's finished, we don't know when they're going to release it, we don't know what it's going to say," Cr Ellsmore said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was unable to confirm a release date, but said the government was in "the process of finalising" the review.

A review into the STRA sector was announced in 2024. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

A spokesperson for the NSW government said any changes to the regulation of short-term accommodation would need to consider impacts on the tourism sector as well as housing affordability.

"The government is currently reviewing the operation of the short-term rental accommodation planning and regulatory framework and will make announcements in due course," they said.

Solutions to the problem 'complex'

Short Term Accommodation Association Australia (STAAA) executive director Keiran Craig-Jones said there was no evidence nightly caps worked and that prohibition would punish compliant operators.

He said the main issue was the rental arbitrage model, where a third party leases a home to sublet it for a significant profit, which was leading to genuine long-term rental housing being lost.

"Those operators are typically not local, have no vested interest in the local area and community and no relationship with the neighbours who deal with the consequences," he said.

The peak body, he said, therefore supported a ban on the practice with a focus on "enforcement, registration and data-sharing" instead.

Caitlin Buckle, a lecturer in City Planning at the University of New South Wales, said stricter regulations may not necessarily encourage property owners to move into the long-term market.

Professor Buckle says really strict regulations may deter people from offering their homes. (Supplied: Anna Kucera)

"Really strict regulations may actually just prevent people from offering their homes to anyone at all rather than them necessarily changing their minds and offering it onto the long-term market," Professor Buckle said.

To regulate the sector effectively, it was important to consider the local area, short-term rental habits, financial feasibility and the reasoning for letting out properties, she explained.

"I think one of the key challenges would be to getting really good data … that's a really important starting place from being able to actually anticipate what different regulations might look like and what the impact of those regulations might be just because it can be very complex," she said.

World.title: City's drinking water diluted after elevated PFAS levels detected
World.content:
The water authority in a southern New South Wales city has assured its supplies are safe to drink, after a dilution program reduced the level of so-called "forever chemicals" found in some of its bores.

Riverina Water said the dilution regime was implemented in December 2025 at two of its West Wagga Wagga raw water bores, after routine testing uncovered "unexpected" levels of PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances).

Riverina Water engineering director Troy Van Berkel said the source of the contamination was unclear.

"An initial desktop study has been carried out to say there is not a single source, it's more multiple sources and potential historic use in the area," he said.

Elevated levels of PFAS have been detected in raw water samples taken from Riverina Water's West Wagga bore number five. (ABC News: Melinda Hayter)

In one instance, the levels of one type of PFAS were almost double the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines in the untreated water, with PFOS in December 2025 measuring at 0.015 nanograms a litre (ng/L).

The guidelines require PFOS levels to be under 0.008ng/L.

Mr Van Berkel said dilution had lowered PFAS levels in its treated water to within Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and it remained safe for consumption.

PFAS are laboratory-made chemicals historically used in firefighting foams, non-stick cookware and water-repellent clothing.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control states some studies have associated PFAS exposure with high cholesterol, lower birth weight in babies, and an increased risk of testicular and kidney cancer.

PFAS testing of Wagga Wagga's water supply is undertaken offsite by an accredited laboratory. (ABC News: Melinda Hayter)

The West Wagga bore field is one of four sources for the city's drinking water.

Riverina Water recently signed a memorandum of understanding with the Department of Defence over the management of its East Wagga bore field, due its proximity to a Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) base where firefighting foams were previously used.

Publicly available data shows PFAS levels at two West Wagga bores have regularly exceeded those at East Wagga.

Mr Van Berkel said the West Wagga contamination was not linked to the RAAF base or the city's other known PFAS contamination site, the Kapooka Military Area.

Troy Van Berkel says the PFAS in the West Wagga bore field is likely coming from multiple sources. (ABC News: Melinda Hayter)

Dilution 'good choice'

Friends of the Earth land use researcher Anthony Amis has been tracking PFAS contamination across Australia.

Mr Amis said the West Wagga results were concerning.

"Even if they're not above the drinking water guidelines, there are still potential impacts that could be occurring with people that consume that water on a regular basis," he said.

Anthony Amis is calling for testing of Wagga Wagga's tap water. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

PFAS remediation researcher associate professor Cheng Zhang, from the Australian Institute for Bioengineering and Nanotechnology at the University of Queensland, said while technologies to remove PFAS from the environment were being developed, they were not widely used.

"Dilution may be a good choice in the meantime to help maintain contamination below the regulation level," he said.

Tap water tests ruled out

Mr Amis's research has focused on wastewater treatment plants.

He believes the Wagga Wagga City Council (WWCC) owned Narrung Street Sewage Treatment Plant is a potential contamination source.

A WWCC spokesperson said quarterly PFAS testing at the plant had been underway since January 2024.

"During this time there have been no measurable indications of PFAS at the Narrung Street Sewage Treatment Plant," they said.

From October, licensed landfills and sewage treatment plants in NSW will be required to monitor and report PFAS in wastewater.

The Narrung Street Sewage Treatment Plant is near the affected bore field. (ABC News: Simon Wallace)

Mr Amis said Wagga's tap water should be tested.

"It's one thing to have it at the treatment plants and another entirely to see what's coming through the taps in people's houses," he said.

Riverina Water said it was more cost effective to test at water sources.

Collaborative management

Riverina Water has not published the results of its PFAS tests, undertaken offsite at an accredited laboratory, since March.

"There's sometimes a delay getting these results and making sure the data validated. The results for those bores have been within Australian Drinking Water Guidelines," Mr Van Berkel said.

Riverina Water said while it will continue its routine PFAS testing, further investigations at the West Wagga bore field were the responsibility of the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA).

A NSW government spokesperson said the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water was aware of "occasionally elevated" PFAS levels in some of West Wagga's bores.

"Threshold exposure levels are very conservative and consider a large margin of safety, which always err on the side of caution," they said.

"The NSW government will continue to work with local water utilities to ensure appropriate long-term measures are in places to effectively manage PFAS risks."

Cheng Zhang says dilution is an effective way of managing PFAS in drinking water supplies. (Supplied: University of Queensland)

Dr Zhang said with more than 14,000 types of PFAS chemicals, there remained significant challenges in managing their impact.

"I always think PFAS issues are both a legacy contamination problem and also an emerging environmental challenge," he said.

"The government should work with researchers, industry and also communities to form clear regulation and invest more in treatment plant infrastructure."

World.title: Penguin bird flu vaccination drive passes 1,000-dose milestone
World.content:
The rush to protect Victoria's little penguin population against bird flu continues, with about 1,000 birds having received their first doses of an H5N1 vaccine.

Authorities plan to vaccinate 5,000 little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda, with hundreds of the birds being rounded up and given a shot each night for the past week.

Last night, a team at the Phillip Island Nature Park, south-east of Melbourne, vaccinated their 1,000th bird, on the same day as the deadly strain that has killed hundreds of birds was detected in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia, the first time it has been confirmed as crossing over to Australia's mammal population.

Phillip Island is home to about 40,000 little penguins, making it the world's largest colony.

Worst-case modelling suggests a major bird flu outbreak could kill between 8,000 and 16,000 of the birds.

About 10,000 doses of the vaccine are needed for the two-shot program.

About 1,000 of the little penguins on Phillip island have been given a dose of the bird flu vaccine so far. (ABC News)

Environment Minister Jaclyn Symes says little penguins that feature in Phillip Island's nightly "parade" will have now had their first dose, with the team to recapture the birds to deliver the second dose in three to four weeks.

"We know that bird flu is here, we know we can't stop it but we want to put the penguin colony in the best possible place to ensure that they are protected as much as possible," Ms Symes said ahead of last night's effort.

Ms Symes said the vaccine would increase the antibodies each bird had but it remained unknown whether it would stop them from catching the flu.

"It will provide a level of protection but importantly, it may provide a level of ability to recover from the disease if it does catch it," she said.

Jaclyn Symes says the vaccination program provides the best possible protection against the bird flu. (ABC News)

Vaccination program thought to be world's first

Phillip Island Nature Parks reserve manager Ben Thomas said the team had been out late each night over the past week, starting at the quieter end of the penguin parade ground before focusing on the busier western end of the parade on Sunday night.

He said as the penguins came up the beach, the team trapped them in an enclosure, then moved them to smaller pens to deliver the vaccine.

The little penguins are herded into holding pens to be vaccinated against bird flu. (ABC News)

"They are feisty little animals; you do go home with a few bites and scratches," he said.

"We're trying to process them as quickly as we can but as gentle and safe as we can to make sure these penguins are happy and healthy."

A team from Phillip Island Nature Parks holds a briefing before last night's little penguin vaccination effort. (ABC News)

Despite taking time to ensure careful handling, Mr Thomas said there was a sense of urgency among the team.

"[The penguins] do live shoulder-to-shoulder so once [the flu] arrives, it may spread quite quickly through the colony."

Ben Thomas says his team is vaccinating hundreds of penguins each night. (ABC News)

Phillip Island Nature Parks CEO Catherine Basterfield said it was the first time the team had attempted anything like this.

She said she also believed it was the first mass vaccination program of this scale in the world.

"It is really tricky and penguins are difficult to handle," Ms Basterfield said.

"Our team took some time earlier in the week in testing, planning, trialling different methods of being able to roll out this vaccination program."

But she said the team was being helped by the habitual characteristics of the little penguins, which returned to the same beach most nights, mostly waddled up the same pathway, returned to the same burrow every night, and were used to human interaction.

Catherine Basterfield says vaccination teams from Phillip Island Nature Parks have been on the beach each night. (ABC News)

Ms Basterfield said the team was confident they would be able to re-capture the same birds in three weeks' time to deliver the crucial follow-up dose.

"This is the world's largest little penguin colony so in terms of the species, it's an amazing opportunity to really protect this stronghold."

World.title: Landslide at Guinea landfill kills at least 30
World.content:
Thirty people have died in Guinea's capital, Conakry, after a mound of rubbish in a landfill collapsed onto neighbouring homes following heavy rains, the government has said.

Six others were seriously injured in the 2:00am Sunday incident in the Dar-es-salam neighbourhood on the capital's outskirts, a government statement said.

"Significant material and human resources have been deployed to search for any people who may still be buried, to rescue the victims and to recover the bodies," the government of the West African country said.

Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah visited the site of the deadly accident, where AFP photographers saw excavators take part in a search-and-rescue operation through the collapsed landfill under the gaze of a crowd of onlookers.

Measures have been taken "to ensure medical care for the wounded" and "assistance for those affected by this tragedy", the government statement said.

Before the official toll's announcement, neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had said he feared that many had died in the collapse.

"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he told AFP.

One of Guinea's main opposition figures, former prime minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident "a tragedy that plunges us into dismay".

Rescue workers search through a heap of refuse. (AP: Fodo Toure)

"This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the dump had been announced for this Sunday, August 23," he said on Facebook.

"It is now up to the competent authorities to establish, with full transparency, the circumstances that led to this disaster and to draw all the necessary conclusions," he added in the statement posted before the release of the death toll.

In recent days, the government had ordered the eviction of people around the site because of fears of a collapse.

Guinea is led by General Mamadi Doumbouya, who came to power in a coup in 2021 before being elected president in December 2025.

AFP

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Hanson intervenes after Farley claims migration target ‘not too different’ from Labor’s; Swans crisis deepens amid fresh allegations of ‘multiple sexual assaults’
World.content:
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has defended his colleague David Farley after Farley’s concession on the ABC yesterday that the party’s headline migration figure would be scarcely different to the Albanese government’s target.

Party leader Pauline Hanson intervened to reject Farley’s assertion in a lengthy social media post yesterday afternoon, insisting: “One Nation’s policy is to cut net overseas migration to 130,000.”

“It’s 130,000 net. We’ve been saying that all along. It’s 130,000 net overseas migration,” Joyce told Seven’s Sunrise this morning.

In his Insiders interview, Farley said this figure did not include a raft of key migrant categories, including Pacific mobility workers and nurses, and that these workers would add at least 100,000 people to the target.

World.title: Government, parents, teachers: ‘It is everyone’s responsibility to be part of combating this culture’
World.content:
NationalViolence Government, parents, teachers: ‘It is everyone’s responsibility to be part of combating this culture’ Samantha Selinger-Morris August 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“This obviously happens every single day in every single postcode in Australia: sexual, family, and domestic violence, but there’s always – every six months, one year, two years – a series of high-profile events that cause a lot of headlines, and then we’re talking about it again,” says sexual consent activist and author Chanel Contos. ‘It’ in this case is sexual violence against women. And ‘it’ has been impossible to ignore. In the past two weeks alone, three young teen students from elite Sydney private all-boys Scots College were arrested and charged with the aggravated sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl, a week later three teens were arrested in south-west Sydney for a string of charges including aggravated sexual assault of a 17-year-old girl, and in the middle was the alleged Sydney Swans sexual assault allegation. These are just the stories that made the news. Elite Sydney all-boys school Scots College. Steven Woodburn “It’s frustrating at this point because it’s not as simple as one solution. There are so many things that need to be done from the government, from parents, from teachers, from individuals, from sporting clubs. It is everyone’s responsibility to be part of combating this culture because if you’re being complacent in it, it kind of makes you complicit in it,” Contos, a leading voice in consent education in Australia, tells The Morning Edition podcast host Samantha Selinger-Morris. It’s clear, Contos says, that while consent education is still critical, sexual violence against women and girls has been heightened by the intersection of explicit and constant access to pornography.



The five Sydney Swans players stood down over the alleged sexual assault investigation. 9News In today’s episode of The Morning Edition, host Selinger-Morris and Contos discuss young men and sexual violence; how elite athletes tend to engage in sexual violence at disproportionately higher rates than the general population; and the relatively new addition of social media algorithms that radicalise boys into misogyny. Click the player below to listen to the full episode, or read on for an edited extract of the conversation. Samantha Selinger-Morris: Well, let’s get into this issue of a particular culture and whether it may or may not foster certain attitudes against women. And I wanted to ask you generally about elite all-male environments in particular, whether they be at school or in sport. Because there have been a couple of studies overseas of college campuses that have found that male athletes or men who sort of exist in all-male environments – such as fraternities or team sports like basketball – that they are overrepresented in reported acts of sexual assault and domestic violence compared to the general student body. So, can you walk us through, if you can, what is it about these environments that perhaps leads to that?



Chanel Contos spoke on The Morning Edition podcast. Jamila Toderas Chanel Contos: I think these institutions matter to everyone, because boys and men who are socialised in them disproportionately go on to hold positions of power in our country and in our economy. And that means the way that they are socialised, whether that’s with apathy or empathy towards certain groups, will dictate how our country runs, how our businesses run, what our parental leave policies are, the culture of institutions, our politicians, like all of these things. You know, we’ve had three prime ministers attend Sydney Grammar, and only one female prime minister. So, just to kind of show again the concentration of power in a select few schools in our country. Related Article Opinion

Crime This moment crystallises a very uncomfortable truth about sexual violence Natassia Chrysanthos Federal political correspondent Well, I think what happens in all-male environments is that boys and men can often be socially rewarded from their peers by three key things: the first being physical ability, which is a spectrum, all the way up until, you know, boys getting in fights on the weekend is the extreme. And then the non-extreme, and the most celebrated by our society, is their physical sporting ability. But the other two things are wealth and sexual conquest, so you can understand how those would interact in these environments when you kind of get social status from being wealthy or from sexual activity with other girls or women. Listen to the full podcast episode in the player above. Hear the story behind the headlines on The Morning Edition podcast, every weekday from 5am on Apple, Spotify or your favourite podcast platform.

World.title: ‘Never mind the Nazis’, Coalition says to the Brethren. ‘Just show us the money’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalExtremism Opinion ‘Never mind the Nazis’, Coalition says to the Brethren. ‘Just show us the money’ Michael Bachelard Senior writer, The Age August 24, 2026 — 6:00am

August 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You’d have thought that even in federal parliament, revelations that a group of Christians paid neo-Nazis to try to sway an election would prompt some introspection. Apparently not if you’re in the federal Coalition. When Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman Lloyd Grimshaw beamed into a hearing of the electoral matters committee on Friday to answer some hard questions, three senior Coalition figures were on hand to dole out Dorothy Dixers and indulge the fantasy that the church was the real victim here. Lloyd Grimshaw, director of Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, appears via video link at the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters. Dominic Lorrimer Now the Liberal Party’s top two figures, Tony Abbott and Angus Taylor, have gone on a nice long bike ride sponsored by one of the church’s charities, the Rapid Relief Team.



Grimshaw’s oleaginous evidence on Friday was that he knew nothing of Nazis and that the revelations in this, masthead – backed by documentary evidence and multiple sources – rose no higher than “gossip”. Related Article Investigations Brethren feed Angus Taylor, Tony Abbott days after Nazi revelations Grimshaw declined an invitation to go on oath to give his evidence – something the Brethren claim is based on scripture. Even with the benefit of that theological escape clause, though, Oily Lloyd couldn’t say with certainty on whose behalf he was speaking. Was it the tiny company/charity that he’s a director of, the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church Ltd? Or was it the church itself, a global, unincorporated fellowship of 50,000 people? This convenient confusion meant that when Grimshaw denied “the church” was responsible for thousands of his co-religionists flooding polling booths at the last federal election, he was probably just talking about his company.





The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church’s charity, the Rapid Relief Team, is a sponsor of the Pollie Pedal bike ride. Facebook The job of Grimshaw and his little company, PBCC Limited, is to give implausible deniability to all this. It’s what he was doing before the committee on Friday. He’s been doing it for years. In 2016, for example, Grimshaw co-signed a “confidentiality deed”. His little company, PBCC Ltd, agreed to pay $920,000 to an overly talkative former church spokesman, who would in return destroy evidence in a defamation case and refuse to testify. The case was over the church’s attempt to cover up the repeated sexual abuse by an elder of a seven-year-old girl. All these things are on the public record because I’ve put them there. What that means is that Grimshaw is not the villain of this piece. He’s just a camp follower obeying his own indoctrination.



The real villains are Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan’s Coalition. Because after Grimshaw slithered back to his day job, their political parties expressed outrage that a parliamentary committee had even dared ask questions of the Brethren church. They demanded the committee chair’s sacking. Then Taylor set off on a Brethren-sponsored bike ride. The fact is, this is all about the money. The Coalition has relied on under-the-table donations from the Brethren for decades. In 2016, NSW ICAC’s Operation Spicer unearthed a document showing $67,230 in donations from the party’s Brethren “friends”, most of them a few dollars under the disclosable threshold. In ICAC now, Operation Rosny is investigating the Catholic Schools NSW’s alleged $265,000 influence-buying campaign with the state Liberals. If a quarter of a million dollars is enough to give rise to an allegation of corruption, public hearings and the full rigmarole, what would ICAC say about the Brethren’s wholesale spending in the attempt to buy the federal government?



If only the National Anti-Corruption Commission had the same legislation and the same energy as ICAC. Maybe then phones would be tapped, public hearings held, and we’d stop soft-soaping this odious church and call the Brethren’s campaign by its proper name – rampant political corruption. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: It’s no surprise to Kath to learn emotions may drive heavy drinking
World.content:
NationalAlcohol It’s no surprise to Kath to learn emotions may drive heavy drinking Wendy Tuohy August 24, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kath Elliott recognises her former self in some of her clients seeking support to change the way they drink. Many are high-performing, aged in their 40s and 50s, with big jobs, families and numerous stress factors. Elliott describes herself as a former “social binge drinker”, able to spend days off alcohol but then going hard. “If I look back at it, a lot of it was around relieving stress and the pressure of juggling motherhood, working a corporate job and trying to keep that perfect veneer,” she says. Kath Elliott recognises many of the reasons her clients seeking support to manage alcohol consumption drink. Eddie Jim Elliott quit alcohol in 2019, aged 46, following a fall in front of her family after drinking. She left corporate PR, trained as an alcohol mindset coach and has since worked with people to understand and adjust their relationship with Australia’s favourite drug.



She helps her clients examine what underlies their alcohol use – shifting from “automatically responding to ‘I need a drink’ to … ‘What am I actually feeling?’” – and has noticed women often identify stress and the sense of reward as factors. Alcohol use has traditionally been researched on males, in part because men have historically been far bigger drinkers and partly because women’s variable hormones were viewed as a complexity, says Dr Leigh Walker, a Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health researcher. Related Article Parenting Are the parents all right? Why raising children feels harder than ever But in recent decades, men’s drinking has declined in Australia and women’s has increased, especially in mid-life, and Walker and others have begun researching what is driving the change. Walker’s team has just published a paper on sex differences in brain circuitry showing emotions are a stronger driver of binge-drinking for females than males. The researchers believe this shows stress or distress may be a cause of craving among female binge drinkers.



“There is building evidence to understand the female brain acts differently in response to alcohol and what causes us to drink excessively. You go out to have one drink, but instead you have five – that stop signal is what we’re interested in,” said Walker, who leads the Florey’s hormones and behaviour group. The brain’s emotional regulation centre was far more strongly activated in females than males while binge-drinking, and when this mechanism was blocked, females consumed less alcohol, the group found. Though for ethical reasons this research needs to be conducted on mice – which like many mammals enjoy alcohol when freely given access to it – the brain mechanisms are relevant across species. ‘Women will drink at levels that many don’t realise are affecting their body in much worse ways [than men face] because of our physiology.’ Dr Leigh Walker, Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health Closing the gender gap in understanding drivers of alcohol consumption is especially important because alcohol causes more severe physical harm to women at lower consumption levels, and women have a higher risk of certain alcohol-related problems than men.



“Women will drink at levels that many don’t realise are affecting their body in much worse ways [than men face] because of our physiology,” Walker said. “We have much more fat, and alcohol can ‘live’ in that fat in a sense; we drink less and get more drunk, and the amount coursing around in our bodies is also different from men because of their lean mass, and how it’s metabolised.” Associate Professor Shalini Arunogiri, an addiction and mental health researcher with Monash University and a treating psychiatrist at Turning Point, said the research finding conformed with what clinicians see. Confirming the link between emotions and alcohol in brain mechanisms was valuable in the quest for better treatments, she said. Dependent drinking and craving for alcohol as a response to stress alone was more clinically common in women than in men, Arunogiri said, while patterns for men included stress and also reward responses. “For a lot of women, the cues are internal: thinking about stress, pain, trauma; struggling to cope is driving the urge to drink as the way to manage that rather than seeing a bottle shop [and sensing reward],” she said.



Women interviewed as part of the Florey’s gender and behaviour lab work on how sex, hormones, and neural circuits shape vulnerability to alcohol-use disorders have spoken about managing the aftermath of trauma with alcohol. “Emotional pain is a big part of what I’ve seen and listen to in people’s stories,” said Walker. Related Article Menopause Hangovers getting worse? Menopause could be to blame “For a lot of people alcohol is a coping mechanism … we are trying to understand comorbid problems like depression and alcohol use, or stress disorders or trauma, why people are drinking, and looking at treatments tailored by sex and gender as well.” Australian and New Zealand women have among the highest rates of risky and binge-drinking globally, Walker said. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows up to one in four women (18 to 24 per cent) binge drinks – more than four drinks on a single occasion – at least once a month.



Australia’s first study into the incidence of female drinking at very high-risk levels, by Flinders University in 2024, found more than 300,000 women regularly drink at such levels, and highlighted growing evidence alcohol may interact with women’s natural biological rhythms and its impact worsens with age and menopause. Arunogiri said the Florey research was important because it provided evidence that might lead to better treatments for alcohol use disorder. “The work presented here is ground-breaking at a mechanistic level. It raises the possibility of future drug development. It helps us understand the nuance in how we view women’s alcohol use,” she said. Kath Elliott said women wanting to cut down on alcohol often tell her similar things about why they drink to what the researchers report. But her personal experience has taught her that managing difficult emotions is far easier without alcohol in her system. “Since I’ve been alcohol-free, I’ve been much more able to cope with stress in a better way,” she said. “You’re able to emotionally regulate so much better using other tools … and by the very nature of taking a toxic substance out of your body, its ability to deal with stress is already increased so much.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Lighten up a bit’: Trump caps US’ 250th birthday with IndyCar race in DC
World.content:
Washington: A cheer goes up from the crowd at Penn Quarter Sports Tavern in downtown Washington, DC. President Donald Trump has appeared on the TV screen, waving from the grandstand with the First Lady. The inaugural IndyCar Freedom 250 Grand Prix might be principally a sporting event, but it is also political. Jeanette Boras and her son, Trent, came from California to attend the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington. Michael Koziol “I’m here to support America,” says Jeanette Boras, 68, who has travelled from California with her son. They also came for Trump’s inauguration and recent July 4 celebrations. “In my personal opinion, Trump is doing an amazing job. He’s bringing people together. I’m just here to support him - to make America great again.”



Crowds packed the streets around Washington’s National Mall on Sunday (US time) for the first IndyCar race to ever take place in the nation’s capital. For 147 laps, they zoomed around the grand Smithsonian museums and hulking government buildings that surround the mall, watched by the lucky 100,000 who scored their free trackside tickets in a lottery. It was the first time a Grand Prix race was held on the streets of the US capital. AP Photo/Nick Wass Crowds faced tight security; the Secret Service ordered people to empty their water bottles before entry. Inside, queues of up to 100 people snaked over the grass waiting for lunch from the “Freedom Grill” – where water was available for $US4.50 a bottle. A beer costs $US14 (and a half-hour wait). Spectators were treated to no fewer than seven military flyovers, including the luxury Boeing 747 that was gifted to Trump by Qatar for use as Air Force One.



Ahead of the race, the president’s motorcade – including the reinforced limousine known as the Beast – took a leisurely lap of honour around the 2.7-kilometre-long course, receiving loud cheers. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum delivered the traditional line: “Gentlemen, start your engines.” Trump waved the green flag to commence racing. President Donald Trump waves the green flag to start the race alongside first lady Melania Trump. Doug Mills/Pool The New York Times via AP It was the capstone event to a summer of celebrations for America’s 250th birthday, including a UFC fight at the White House, the Great American State Fair and a record-breaking fireworks display on July 4. The events were organised by Freedom250, an outfit established by the Trump administration to essentially take over from America250, a bipartisan organisation set up by Congress, and provide more patriotic, Trump-aligned programming.



First lady Melania Trump – a racing fan whose father took her to Formula 1 events when she was growing up in Europe – helped tie the event to her foster youth initiative, Fostering the Future. “It’s an incredible day,” she told broadcast partner Fox. “I loved every minute of it.” Loading House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson called the event “pure Americana” and said Washington should host the event again next year. Burgum told Fox it was a strong possibility. “Hotels, restaurants, the people of Washington DC, the greater capital region all love this idea,” Burgum said. “Everybody I’ve met has said, ‘Please, please do this again next year’.”



Even so, some Washington residents grumbled about their city being turned into a racetrack. In the heavily Democratic capital, anything linked to Trump is generally viewed with deep scepticism. And politics is inescapable, even at the Grand Prix. Outside Archives subway station, four older white women held a long banner that said: “MAGA: When was America ever great before for anyone but us white folk?” Erika Berg, holding the banner on the left, said she and her fellow white women were protesting white supremacy. Michael Koziol One of the women, 68-year-old Erika Berg, objected to the idea that the US was marking 250 years of freedom. “That’s white supremacy because 4 million African Americans were not freed until 1865,” she said. “So, anyone who echoes that tagline, anyone who is ignorant of that history, is a bona fide white supremacist.”



Berg said her protest had received a mixed reception. Young white men tended to yell and swear at them, she said, while some people of colour would come up and “whisper” a thank-you. “It’s truth-telling,” she said. “I feel like that’s what we’re doing here today – we are honouring the ancestors whose land was stolen, whose labour was stolen, whose bodies were stolen.” “Lighten up a little bit”: Marlon Cienfuegos from Maryland at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington. Michael Koziol But not everyone thought the IndyCar race was the best forum for politics. Back at the Penn Quarter Sports Tavern, Marlon Cienfuegos – wearing his Washington Grand Prix T-shirt and Speedway Slammer cap – just wanted to admire the flyovers and the cars. “It’s once in a lifetime,” said the 35-year-old from nearby Maryland. “It’s the only 250th birthday we’re gonna have, so you gotta make the most of it.”



Cienfuegos said some people were always going to complain. “Where there’s white, there’s black ... Instead, they should maybe walk out and talk to people they don’t know, people that are here for the first time. Make some friends. Lighten up a little bit. It’s a good time.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Brethren feed Angus Taylor, Tony Abbott days after Nazi revelations
World.content:
PoliticsFederalInvestigations Brethren feed Angus Taylor, Tony Abbott days after Nazi revelations Michael Bachelard August 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Liberal Party federal president Tony Abbott are enjoying the hospitality of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church this week despite evidence that its elders paid neo-Nazi affiliates and far-right figures to bully and intimidate politicians at the last election. Pollie Pedal 2026 riders. The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church’s charity, the Rapid Relief Team, is a sponsor of the ride, which this year is raising funds for SAS veterans charity Wandering Warriors and their families. Instagram The church’s public-facing charity, the Rapid Relief Team, is a major sponsor of Abbott and Taylor’s annual Pollie Pedal bike ride, providing breakfast every day of the eight-day tour, which set off from Toowoomba on Saturday. Taylor, who fell off his bike on the first day of the ride, distanced himself from any alleged criminality as part of the Brethren’s campaign and said, “all members of Pollie Pedal are grateful for RRT’s contribution”. The church’s members do not vote, and will not eat, befriend or socialise with outsiders under their “doctrine of separation”, but Taylor has previously said the charity plays “an enormously important role in our community”.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor fell off his bike on this year’s annual Pollie Pedal. There is no suggestion that Abbott or Taylor knew of or supported the Brethren payments to far-right figures. But after this masthead revealed these details of the Brethren campaign, Byron Fay, executive director of political funding group Climate 200, referred the church to the The Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission for investigation. Climate 200, a key financial supporter of teal candidates and a victim of a Brethren-sponsored far-right stunt, asked the commission to probe whether the church or “registered charities operating under or alongside its institutional umbrella” had broken the law. Promoting or opposing a political party or a candidate for office, and conducting activities that are “contrary to public policy or unlawful” are outlawed under the charities legislation. More than a dozen Brethren-linked charities have tax-free net assets of more than $295 million – significantly more than Oxfam and Save The Children combined, once their government-funded private school network is included.



Almost all their activities are directed towards helping their own members, not the public. The church’s spokesman, Lloyd Grimshaw, on Friday denied before a parliamentary committee the church had anything to do with commissioning or paying for the far-right stunts, or election campaign canvassing in general. Loading Calling it “bizarre” that he was required to answer questions on the matter, he said the thousands-strong, co-ordinated effort at polling booths by Brethren members was simply a volunteering exercise by individual parishioners. Climate 200 disagreed in its letter to the charities commission. “The synchronised scale, geographic uniformity, and organisational backing suggest institutional co-ordination rather than purely independent, individual volunteering,” Fay wrote in his complaint.



The chair of the Joint Select Committee on Electoral Matters, Labor MP Jerome Laxale, who is leading the grilling of the church over its election involvement, told this masthead that Grimshaw’s evidence before the committee “leaves me with more questions than answers”. Lloyd Grimshaw, director of Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, appears via video link at the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters. Dominic Lorrimer Grimshaw told the committee he represented a small charity called Plymouth Brethren Christian Church Limited, not the church fellowship itself. Laxale said this “puts huge limits around the church’s denials”. “Hiding behind a narrow definition does not circumvent the requirement for all witnesses to answer questions truthfully,” Laxale said. “The giving of false or misleading evidence is a serious matter, and may be regarded as a contempt of parliament.” However, after the hearing, the Coalition doubled down on its support for the controversial church. A group of seven MPs, including Nationals leader Matt Canavan, three shadow ministers and senators from five states issued a joint statement describing the inquiry into the Brethren’s activities as a “hyperpartisan witch hunt” by Labor.



The three-page statement described the inquiry as “persecution”, “madness” and a “disgraceful fiasco” and it called for Laxale to be sacked as committee chair. “Labor’s attacks smack of religious discrimination and are an assault on the basic democratic rights of all Australians,” Canavan wrote. NSW senator Jess Collins said: “We’re another step closer to Albanese’s communist utopia, where religious freedom is not tolerated.”



The Liberal Party’s own review into the election found its members were too old to volunteer on booths, so “some campaigns were grateful for the assistance” of the separatist Brethren church “support group”. Related Article Exclusive

Investigations Exclusive Brethren secretly paid far-right activists to perform stunts disrupting the federal election The Rapid Relief Team confirmed in a Facebook post that it would follow the Pollie Pedal bike ride through “eight locations as riders take on the eight-day journey”. “We’re looking forward to being part of Pollie Pedal for another year and helping keep riders fuelled along the way.” The RRT is the church’s only charity that provides a service to outsiders. It was set up with the help of a public relations firm in 2012 and 2013 after the British charities commission began questioning the Brethren’s tax-free status because it did not provide a public benefit.



RRT’s founding helped the church regain charitable status in Britain. However, it also has a political purpose. In internal church documents, Brethren members are told they are to “engage with a person of influence or status at a local level” to curry favour. Last summer, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was photographed at an RRT tent at the Victorian bushfires – a fact Grimshaw pointed out during his evidence before the parliamentary committee. The prime minister’s office declined to comment. The Plymouth Brethren Christian Church’s Rapid Relief Team Facebook post featuring Anthony Albanese in January. Facebook In Victoria, the Liberal and National parties have both left open the possibility of working with the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church at November’s state election, saying they do not screen volunteers for their religious beliefs.



One Nation’s state leader, Warren Pickering, said he had not been approached by the Brethren with an offer of help but that he would “engage in good faith with all community groups and organisations that reach out”. World.title: ASX set to rise as Wall Street advances; $A, bitcoin stronger
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise as Wall Street advances; $A, bitcoin stronger Stan Choe August 24, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks rose and trimmed their losses from a shaky week. That was even though the bond market, which has been the centre of Wall Street’s action, remained jumpy and continued to add pressure. The S&P 500 rose 0.4 per cent for just its second gain in the six days since setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones jumped 517 points, or 1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.4 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures on Saturday pointing to a gain of 41 points or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.64¢. Reporting season continues with Ampol and Bendigo and Adelaide Bank among the companies set to report results today. Markets are waiting for a breakthrough in the Middle East. AP Ross Stores helped lead the way and rose 4.4 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Jim Conroy said it saw both an increase in new customers and more interest from existing customers, while the off-price retailer at the same time benefited from refunds on tariffs.



Most US companies have reported bigger profits for the spring than analysts expected, which has helped drive stocks to records recently. Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. Related Article Analysis

Home loans ‘Frighteningly easy’: How fake AI payslips fuel mortgage fraud Hopes for continued profit growth got a boost from a preliminary report by S&P Global suggesting growth for US business activity hit a 52-month high. But the other big lever that helps set stock prices, interest rates, has been much shakier. After soaring through the summer and then hesitating following this week’s surprise move by the US Treasury Department to repurchase more US government bonds, yields climbed further on Friday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.73 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Thursday. It’s back above its level from before the Treasury market made its move, which analysts said at the time would likely have only a temporary effect. The 30-year Treasury yield, which the Fed is also targeting with its bond repurchases, also rose and is near its highest level since 2007.



Contributing to Friday’s gains for bond yields was continued uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. That caused oil prices to rise, which affects Treasury yields because they increase worries about inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil settled at $US92.67, up 0.8 per cent. Besides inflation, concerns about the fast-rising debt for the US government have also been sending yields upward. Higher yields can slow the economy and undercut prices for all kinds of investments. One of the biggest beneficiaries of US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s move to try to get longer-term yields lower is bitcoin. Cryptocurrencies often rise when interest rates are lower and more money is flowing through the financial system. Hopes for legislation in Washington to help the crypto industry have also helped it. Bitcoin has climbed above $US77,000 from less than $US63,000 a week ago. That helped stocks in the crypto industry lead Wall Street. Robinhood Markets jumped 13.7 per cent, and Coinbase Global gained 8.2 per cent.



The price of gold also climbed and briefly topped $4,690 per ounce from less than $4,440 a week earlier. The Treasury Department’s buyback announcement has helped weaken the US dollar’s value against other currencies, which tends to give gold’s price a boost. That helped drive stocks of miners higher. Newmont climbed 3.1 per cent, and Freeport-McMoRan jumped 7.6 per cent. Related Article Energy Labor’s plan to reserve more domestic gas stirs hopes of a revival They helped offset a 5.2 per cent drop for OSI Systems, which sells security screening equipment to airports and other specialised electronic systems. It reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, and CEO Ajay Mehra said it was hurt by “the Middle East conflicts which shifted the timing of certain planned deliveries.” Boston Beer sank 2.6 per cent after the seller of Samuel Adams and Dogfish Head said its chief financial officer is leaving the company and announced an interim replacement.



All told, the S&P 500 rose 33.21 points to 7,674.37. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 517.80 to 53,277.01, and the Nasdaq composite added 113.29 to 26,180.45. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in much of Asia and Europe. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 1.2 per cent, and South Korea’s Kospi climbed 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: The plan to divert more patients from Sydney’s busiest emergency rooms
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare The plan to divert more patients from Sydney’s busiest emergency rooms Megan Gorrey August 24, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Emergency department short-stay units will be expanded at six hospitals in Sydney and regional NSW, under a $130 million state government plan to help ease overcrowding and shorten wait times. An extra 22 spaces for patients requiring short-term observation and quick treatment will be delivered at emergency wards at St George, Campbelltown, Nepean, Maitland, John Hunter and Wyong hospitals in the next 12 months. Up to eight more spots will be added the following year. Emergency departments in NSW hospitals are under pressure, particularly in fast-growing areas. James Brickwood Premier Chris Minns said the extra spaces were intended to ease stress on some of the state’s busiest emergency departments, which were experiencing “constant and sustained pressure”. “We know we’ve had some success with these units across the state including the ones we expanded at Campbelltown, Maitland, Wyong and Wollongong hospitals,” he said.



Related Article Hospitals The billion-dollar Sydney hospital that’s performing worse than ever “At hospitals which already have a short-stay unit in the emergency departments, we’re seeing patients with semi-urgent conditions treated and back home quicker without needing to be admitted to a traditional ward in most cases.” The short-stay units provide dedicated spaces for patients who have been triaged and assessed by emergency department staff and require care, observation and treatment for between four and 24 hours. Patients typically require help for semi-urgent conditions such as minor head injuries, allergic reactions, low-risk chest pain, asthma, minor infections or rehydration. The units mean they remain under the care of emergency staff rather than being moved to a general ward, speeding up processing in the emergency room and keeping beds free for very sick patients.



NSW public hospitals had recorded more than half a million admissions to emergency department short-stay units since January 2024, the government said, underscoring their critical role in aiding patient flow, reducing pressure on emergency wards and providing timely access to care. St George Hospital clinical nurse consultant Rochelle Cummins said the Kogarah facility’s existing short-stay unit of 12 beds and treatment chairs had helped to move more stable patients out of the emergency ward, freeing up acute beds and keeping them from being admitted to other wards. Westmead Hospital has an emergency short-stay unit designed to treat semi-urgent patients and free up acute beds. Wolter Peeters “Generally, our short-stay unit is full, so any additional spaces are welcomed and would create capacity within our emergency department to move patients out of the ED and improve flow,” Cummins said. The units offer tests and treatments and allied health support, such as physiotherapy.
