World.title: NZ tobacco policymaking on based media optics, rather than international law - research
World.content:
*This story has been updated with comment from Labour stating Ayesha Verrall had never knowingly met with tobacco industry representatives

New Zealand politicians are basing tobacco policymaking on media optics, rather than international law meant to protect against industry lobbying, new research suggests.

Dr Melissa-Jade Gregan from the University of Auckland said that New Zealand was a signatory to a legally binding international treaty - the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control.

"Our research found that the government has never properly implemented Article 5.3 of the treaty, which requires the protection of health policies against tobacco industry interference," she said.

"Article 5.3 guidelines provide 34 measures to apply across government to all involved in health policymaking, yet implementation here is largely confined to one: tobacco industry meeting registers at the Ministry of Health and Customs. Everyone else falls outside this one protection."

Researchers interviewed 21 politicians, officials, political journalists and public health experts, and analysed government and tobacco industry documents, Gregan said.

"Politicians we spoke to, including those involved in tobacco control policymaking, had limited knowledge of Article 5.3. One openly admitted being ignorant of Article 5.3," she said.

"Considerations about whether to interact with industry were based on media optics rather than legal requirements of the international treaty. Rules that are unknown cannot protect anything."

Gregan said New Zealand needed to enshrine Article 5.3 measures into law and apply protections to everyone involved in health policymaking, including MPs,

The minister responsible for reducing smoking - Associate Health Minister Casey Costello - said that Ministry of Health officials had not raised the issue as a concern.

"If there are parts of the convention that New Zealand hasn't formalised, that approach would have been in place for some time as no changes have been made by this government," she said.

Responding to references to 'politicians involved in tobacco control policy', Costello reiterated that she was the minister responsible for reducing smoking and the policies that support that in the current government.

"I am aware of my obligations and I have not met with anyone from the tobacco industry...The only health minister I am aware of that has is [Labour's] Ayesha Verrall,"' she said. A Labour Party spokesperson said Verrall had never knowingly met with tobacco industry representatives. The spokesperson said Verrall had a member's bill in the ballot to address the issue of policymakers ignoring Article 5.3.

"New Zealand has a small, open government with ministers' diaries released and other forms of scrutiny available and I'm not sure that focusing on the detail of international law is the priority in this space," Costello said.

World.title: Mayors left disappointed by National ruling out bed tax
World.content:
Queenstown contemplates future of accommodation levy Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The Auckland and Queenstown Lakes District mayors are both disappointed with National's announcement on Sunday ruling out the bed tax, with Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown hitting out at National "walking away" from its commitment to the Auckland Regional Deal.

On Sunday, the National Party ruled out the idea of a bed tax, promising that there will be "no new taxes" if it's re-elected.

It comes a fortnight after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke publicly about the possibility of three new taxes under National - a bed tax, a bank tax and a fuel excise increase.

Brown said in a statement that Sunday's announcement raised serious questions about the government's commitment to the regional deal.

"The deal is meaningless if the government cannot honour even a relatively modest commitment to explore an agreed proposal.

"Ruling out the bed-night levy without offering any meaningful alternative to support the industry is deeply disappointing," he said.

The regional deal, signed in April this year, included the government committing to considering the accommodation levy policy in 2027.

Brown said the bed-night levy was a user charge, not a general tax.

"Taxes are unavoidable - you can avoid this by just not staying in a hotel.

"It would result in no additional rates or taxes on Aucklanders, while enabling Auckland to attract more events, support local businesses and grow the regional economy," he said.

Brown said the regional deal was an agreement between the Crown and the council.

"It should not be something one party can simply disregard."

Brown said he looked forward to discussing the issue with ministers responsible for the regional deal - Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop and Local Government Minister Simon Watts - at the next quarterly review of progress in September.

Luxon looking at 'other options'

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Speaking to Morning Report on Monday, Luxon denied reneging on both the signed deal with Auckland and the as-yet-unsigned one with Queenstown Lakes just for a clearer tax policy position.

"We were talking about exploring an accommodation levy to deal with the pressures and the costs associated with tourism in those regions.... we need to deal with it. We will deal with it, but we'll deal about it in a different way."

Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

He said National had looked at the bed tax idea, but "there's just no other way that... a couple setting off for a weekend in Queenstown or Auckland are not going to end up paying that bed tax.

"We're not the party that wants to chuck taxes or costs, unnecessary costs, on New Zealanders - and so that's why we say no new taxes."

Host Ingrid Hipkiss pressed Luxon on why he had reneged on the deal with Auckland.

"Because as part of exploring an accommodation levy, there's lots of other options that you would be exploring at the same time as well," he said.

Hipkiss replied: "Well, put those in the deal as well, put those in the agreement as well."

Luxon said that "as part of an exploration process, that's what we would be doing".

He would not say what other options National would consider, saying he did not want to "predetermine outcomes", but there were several options.

"We'll work with the councils and the mayors on that, but what we're not going to do - not going to do - is actually introduce a cost and a tax on New Zealanders that actually they end up paying rather than the tourists.

"We're very committed to finding the solution through that, and we need to do that because we've got some real pressure from tourism in some parts of the country - we're deeply, deeply committed to it, but we're also deeply committed to not having Kiwis pay a tax."

A 'complete u-turn'

Queenstown Lakes District Mayor John Glover told RNZ it appeared to be a "complete u-turn", after the government agreed to consider the accommodation levy for visitors in both the already-signed Auckland Regional Deal, and the deal for his region, which was almost signed a week-and-a-half ago - but had to be rescheduled due to National's crisis talks on the same day.

"It feels like policy making in a state of panic. I appreciate there's a campaign message about no new taxes, but the government particularly says it doesn't want to tax Kiwis for a weekend away.

"Well, what we just need to be clear about is that Kiwis are already being heavily taxed across the country, because every ratepayer that's in a tourism town is already having to pay for the cost of tourism, so to say they don't want Kiwis to be taxed is a bit of a rabbit hole to be going down," he said.

Glover said not being able to implement a bed tax would be "significant" for his region, where infrastructure was strained by the number of visitors each year - doubling the population during peaks.

"Things like car parks or waste collection, you know we've got some really expensive roads that go to the likes of the Routeburn track or Skippers Canyon, there might be five ratepayers live down there, but tens of thousands of visitors go there every year," he said.

"You would think we deserve governments that support tourism in this country, and they need to give council the tools to do that," Glover added.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said she was "surprised" with the announcement, considering that the bed tax formed part of the Auckland Regional Deal.

"We're definitely sad to hear that because there's been so much hard work behind the scenes," she said.

"Councils without any alternative will have to continue to use ratepayer funds to invest in tourism offering," she added.

World.title: Opportunity leader: Voters starting to see us as a stable and safe coalition partner
World.content:
Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The leader of the Opportunity Party says people are starting to see the nascent movement as a stable and safe coalition partner, as the new RNZ-Reid Research poll puts the party in the driver's seat.

Meanwhile Labour has been unable to capitalise on National's recent woes, and has actually been the one to suffer.

But Chris Hipkins believes National's attack line on tax will only weaken as the campaign ramps up.

Opportunity is on 5.3 percent in the latest poll, the party cracking the threshold needed to enter Parliament for the first time in this poll.

Opportunity Party is in the kingmaker position - poll Morning Report Download MP3 4m

If the results were replicated on polling day, the right bloc would have 59 seats and the left 55 - neither having the numbers to govern without Opportunity's 6.

Leader Qiulae Wong said there was a growing discontent amongst New Zealanders that the major parties were not setting out a vision for the future.

"We're providing an alternative narrative around what that could be, and I think New Zealanders are really, really ready for that. So I think that's where we're seeing interest grow in Opportunity," she told RNZ.

National has ruled out working with Opportunity, and is starting to lump its policies in with Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori.

But Opportunity is leaving the door open to National.

Labour, meanwhile, is keeping Opportunity as an option, but Hipkins is not going to give Wong a ring before the election.

"We don't do any deals pre-election," he said.

"My view is that voters get the chance to have their say first, and then we sit down and we talk to other parties after the election, depending on what the voters dish up."

Wong, too, did not see the point in doing any deals now.

"I don't think it's helpful for us to try and play into the left-right blocs. That's what we're trying to move away from. We've said that we'll set out clear bottom lines, so that will give those major parties an indication of how we'll approach negotiations. Then it's really up to them. Once we see how the votes fall, how they want to respond to that."

Labour's 1.8 point drop to 32.2 percent comes as National ramps up the attacks, hitting Labour where it is most vulnerable: tax.

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown was less willing to talk about National's 29.1 percent result than he was going after Labour on tax, saying tax would be the key issue at this year's election.

"What this poll shows is that as New Zealanders realise that Labour and their mates are intent on increasing taxes, they are becoming more and more concerned about that agenda."

Hipkins said a "scare campaign" was all National had, and it would quickly be found out.

"They can't campaign on their track record because their track record is so abysmal. So if their strategy for getting re-elected is just to make up lies about the opposition, I think that people will soon see through that."

Brown was adamant National would not work with Opportunity, rolling out the tax attack again.

"We're not going to be doing a deal with Opportunity. They want to put a land tax on every single New Zealander."

Simeon Brown, left, is doubling down on National's vow not to work with Opportunity. Supplied

Wong did not believe National's decision to rule Opportunity out had necessarily driven its polling increase, with support coming from the traditional left and right.

"I suppose for many of those people that are supporting us, they see us as the most stable and safe coalition partner, regardless of whether it's a Labour or National-led government."

ACT leader David Seymour remained sceptical, believing Opportunity would run out of steam as more sunlight was shone on the party and its policies.

"They finally come under some scrutiny and basically abandon three of their key policies, under scrutiny, in a couple of weeks. I think that people are starting to look harder at them and seeing less and less as they look harder."

Wong said it was right for Opportunity to come under more scrutiny as it became a viable party for entering Parliament.

"We definitely welcome that. I think for us, we maintain our integrity, we answer questions honestly. We are a party that follows evidence and data, and so we will always engage in conversations in that way," she said.

ACT has attracted some star power in the shape of Paul Henry, but that big name and big personality has not shifted the dial, the party riding steady on 7.7 percent.

Paul Henry speaks at ACT's South Island campaign launch. RNZ

But Seymour said it varied from poll to poll.

"It depends which poll you look at. In others, we've gone up 50 percent, from 6 points to 9 in a month. So I guess you can't really accept the premise that that's true," Seymour said.

"We're very grateful for the people giving their party vote to ACT, and we're going to keep campaigning to lock Labour out and unlock New Zealand's potential right til the final whistle."

The Green Party is also steady on 10.2, eager to put the tumultuous times of the beginning of the term in the past.

MP Ricardo Menéndez March said the party was aiming for its best ever result, and it was building a campaign bigger than ever before.

"This is a really good place for us to build on, in the hope that we can actually secure a record election result come the election."

Menéndez March said the Greens were not relying on Opportunity to change the government.

"The Opportunity Party is relying on being able to potentially keep Luxon in power, which is something we're actively fighting against. And this is why we'll just make sure that we have the biggest vote available to us, so that we actually can secure a change of government and a change of direction."

Te Pāti Māori, meanwhile, is on 3 percent, but that number does not matter to the party anyway as it tells its supporters it wants their candidate votes.

Co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said there would always be supporters who two-ticked Te Pāti Māori, but its focus was on winning the seven Māori seats.

"It's great to have that growing support, but our success is going to be measured by the Māori seats and the influence we can have on on being able to change this government."

And despite comments towards the Greens' Lawrence Xu-Nan that earned him a rebuke from the prime minister, Winston Peters and New Zealand First have not been punished in the polls.

The party is up to 11.9 percent, another consecutive rise.

Peters' response to RNZ was the same as always, that he would turn the polls into confetti.

No rethink on Opportunity - Luxon

Speaking to Morning Report on Monday, Luxon said he did not need to rethink ruling out working with Opportunity.

"No, absolutely not. I mean they want to institute a land tax at 1.75 percent and just be a disaster for every young person who's saved up and put their equity together and gone and secured a home and it gets wiped out immediately.

"They're a party of more tax just like Labour, just like Te Pāti Māori, just like the Greens."

He said the 7 November election was "the poll that matters", and maintained his position laid out last month of not working with Opportunity even under a confidence and supply arrangement.

"When you seriously want to level a 1.75 percent annual land tax on the value of your land that's a big problem."

He said "Labour and their mates" wanted to bring in nine new taxes, despite Labour ruling out bringing in new taxes other than the narrow capital gains tax the party is campaigning on.

National over the weekend https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/1083119/national-promises-no-new-taxes-if-re-elected ruled out any new taxes] - including ideas the government had previously been considering like on banks and a "bed tax" which the government https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/1092926/mayors-left-disappointed-by-national-ruling-out-bed- had agreed to investigate] as part of the signed regional deal with Auckland and the unsigned on with Queenstown Lakes.

World.title: 'An absolute waste': Police officer remains in ICU after being hit by vehicle
World.content:
Police respond to two accidents in Manawatu over weekend Morning Report Download MP3 5m

A senior police officer says he stood at the bedside of a critically injured colleague in despair over the weekend, listening to machines whirring and thought "what an absolute waste".

In the early hours of Saturday morning, the young policeman was allegedly hit by a fleeing driver in Palmerston North as he lay road spikes.

It was not the only incident in the region - with another man critically injured after being hit by a car in Feilding just two hours earlier. The driver fled the scene, police said.

The injured policeman was flown to Wellington Hospital, where he remains in intensive care.

On Monday, Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett told Morning Report the officer was in a stable condition but remained on a ventilator.

"It's a time (to) wait and see as time heals him."

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett. NZ Police

Bennett said the two people in the vehicle that allegedly hit the officer are 14 and 15 years old.

They are facing a "raft of charges", including theft of a vehicle and reckless driving causing injury - an offence that carried "significant and serious penalty", he said.

Bennett said despair came to mind when he thought about the injured men.

"I stood at the bedside of our officer yesterday with his family and as we watched and listened to the machines whirring and uh, you stand there and think 'what an absolute waste'. This could be avoided. The behaviour of the drivers in both incidents is not acceptable and this is a tragic event for the two families involved but also for all of Manawatū."

Bennett said police staff were "getting on with business and acting professional".

However, this was a sadness hanging over the officer's team and wider team "as we wait for some positive news about how he's doing and whether his recovery is going to be successful".

Injured man remains in ICU

Bennett said the man hit by a vehicle in Fielding also remained in ICU on a ventilator.

He said two separate inquiries were being carried out and would determine in the incidents were connected.

At this stage, it didn't appear they were - with one incident involving a fleeing driver and the other involving "anti-social illegal road users".

Bennett told Morning Report the region had a history of serious and violent interactions with boy racers and it wasn't a challenge police would back away from.

World.title: National's pain is no gain for Labour in latest RNZ-Reid Research poll
World.content:
Opportunity Party as kingmaker in new RNZ-Reid Research poll Morning Report Download MP3 11m

Analysis - In normal times, National would be panic-stations after a sub-30 percent poll, with no path to power, and a leader who's never been less popular.

But these are far from normal times.

After the last few weeks' turmoil, the party would have been braced for an even uglier result.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll isn't a ringing endorsement for the coalition government by any means.

The three governing parties are mostly unchanged from the last poll in July and unable to form a government, the prime minister's personal popularity is worse, and a growing number of voters think the country is on the wrong track.

With all of that going on it defies logic an alternative Labour-led government wasn't able to capitalise and make a case for being in power. Even more strikingly, Labour wasn't able to snatch any votes off National in the process.

It points to National's 29.1 percent in this poll now being baked in for the party - a portion of voters who will vote blue through thick and thin and have a high tolerance for party in-fighting and destabilisation, or are so tuned out of politics the headlines of late completely escaped them.

On top of that Christopher Luxon's personal favourability is continuing on its downward decline since he took over as leader, his net performance registering -22.9 percent, and rating behind Chris Hipkins on preferred prime minister with 19.9 percent to the Labour leader's 21.3 percent.

Opportunity Party is in the kingmaker position - poll Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Rounding out the trio of bad news for National was voters feeling like the country is headed in a worse direction than it was in the same poll last month (a net score of -20.9 to July's -11.8).

The other wrinkle in this poll is the success of Opportunity, which has crossed the five percent threshold and now has the balance of power.

Luxon ruled out Opportunity a few weeks ago with a captain's call that started the ball rolling on discontent within his caucus.

RNZ's poll gives the party six seats and hands it the 'kingmaker' title with neither the left nor right bloc able to form a government without it.

If those numbers were replicated on November 7 nobody believes Luxon wouldn't pick up the phone to try get a deal done.

In Hipkins' case, by not explicitly ruling out Opportunity like he has New Zealand First, he has left the door wide open to it.

In a perfect world for Labour it would peel at least some votes off National as well as disgruntled NZ First voters unhappy with the focus on the fringe newcomers to the party.

That would strengthen the Labour vote and allow it to form a coalition with the help of the Greens and Opportunity, and cut Te Pāti Māori out of the frame.

Hipkins knows the policies and political plays of Te Pāti Māori are a handbrake on collecting some of the more centrist Labour vote.

While Labour won't do any deals with Opportunity or signal as much to voters, it's clearly its preferred path to power.

The alternative on current polling is a four-party coalition for either side of the political divide.

Luxon has already shown this term the political management required to keep three parties on the same page, and how easily it can derail.

Add another party to the mix and the role of prime minister could start to look less like running the country and more like herding cats.

The growing influence of the minor parties has been born out of the shrinking purple vote - National and Labour's combined vote - an international trend where the two major parties are giving way to more complex coalition governing arrangements.

In this month's RNZ-Reid Research poll the combined National/Labour vote was 61.3 percent, down on 62.7 percent in July's poll.

The minor parties are now pushing 40 percent of the vote share and the undecided/don't know/would not vote category is down below five percent.

World.title: Police consider charges after violent North Shore group attack on teen girls
World.content:
Police are yet to confirm what charges will be laid over a violent assault on two teenage girls on Auckland's North Shore on Saturday night.

They said they had identified most of the youths involved in the attack, aged bteween 12 and 17.

It is understood the victims had been hanging out with the group around Takapuna on Saturday evening, before the group turned on them at around 9.30pm.

"The victims were separated and reportedly violently assaulted, before having their personal items stolen," Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams said.

The girls were able to identify a number of young people of interest at a bus station.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

In a statement on Sunday, Williams said follow-up enquiries were being made and potential charges were being considered.

World.title: Fijian lawmakers repeal Bainimarama-era surfing law despite opposition criticism
World.content:
Fiji's lawmakers have repealed a 2010 law that opened all surfing breaks to public access, despite opposition criticism that the replacement legislation is "flawed".

The move comes after the Fijian parliament passed the Commercial Use of Marine Areas (CUMA) Bill 2025 last Thursday. The legislation received 27 votes in favour, seven abstentions, and 21 MPs did not vote.

The legislation grants customary owners greater rights over the commercial use of marine areas.

Fiji's coalition government has long signalled it would repeal the Bainimarama-era Regulation of Surfing Areas Act, arguing that customary owners should be compensated for the commercial use of their marine areas.

Deputy Prime Minister Viliame Gavoka, who is also the Tourism Minister, said during the parliamentary debate that the new law offers certainty for investors and fairness for customary owners.

He said the legislation does not undermine investor confidence, as critics have argued.

"We cannot create a framework that recognises customary interest on one hand, but on the other hand, makes the underlying tourism business commercially unviable. When the business fails, no one benefits," he said.

World.title: Dilworth child sex offender must wait six months before moving into home near school, kindergarten.
World.content:
Concern about release of Dilworth School child sex offender Morning Report Download MP3 3m

One of Dilworth School's most prolific child sex offenders owns a home less than 250 metres from a school and kindergarten, and will be allowed to move back six months after his release from prison.

Dilworth's former assistant principal, scoutmaster and history teacher Ian Robert Wilson has been in prison for the past five years for sexual offending against boys between the ages of 12 and 16 years old.

The Parole Board declined his seventh attempt at an early release after he waived he rights to appear before it.

Instead, special conditions have been set for his 22 September release, including that Wilson - now in his 70s - not live at the property he owns for six-months after he is let out of prison.

Wilson was the first sex offender from the infamous school scandal to be sentenced for his crimes.

RNZ understands he owns a home just blocks away from a kindergarten and a school.

Neil Harding is a survivor of Wilson's offending and has waived his automatic right to name suppression in order to speak out.

He addressed the parole board in July for the seventh time, urging them not to release Wilson early.

Harding said Wilson should spend every day of his remaining sentence in prison.

"The children of New Zealand should not be put at risk any earlier than they already are by his impending release," he said.

"To me this man is a monster, who took away my innocence. He is a manipulator, a snake and given the opportunity would take another boy's innocence… in a heartbeat."

Speaking to RNZ, Harding said he genuinely feared for children in the community.

He believes "little boys are still vulnerable" around Wilson.

"Being so close to a school, a kindergarten - I have a real genuine fear [for] their safety."

Harding was urging parents to teach their children about "stranger danger".

"This man is a master manipulator, grooms, and there's a number of Dilworth victims that know exactly what this man can do."

"We just don't want anything that happened to us to happen to another little boy in his neighbourhood," Harding said.

Special release conditions mean Wilson will be unable to return to his property for six months after his release.

Parole Board chair and retired High Court Justice Jan-Marie Doogue told RNZ the board may choose to impose additional special conditions for up to six months, to help reduce the risk of reoffending, support rehabilitation, and protect the community.

It was up to the Department of Corrections, however, to approve Wilson's address.

"This person is not being released to this address," Corrections director of communities, partnerships and pathways Simon Chaplin said.

"They will be managed at a well-established existing supported accommodation property based elsewhere on their release."

Chaplin said Wilson would be closely managed by experienced Corrections staff for the duration of his release conditions, being six months.

"If they do not comply with the conditions set out by the New Zealand Parole Board, we will take action," Chaplin said.

But Corrections noted after the six-month period following Wilson's release, it was unable to legally direct where he could and could not live.

It said no decisions had been made about notifying the nearby school or kindergarten.

Wilson was also ordered not to communicate with or have contact with anyone under the age of 16 unless approved by a probation officer as part of his special release conditions.

History of Child Abuse

Wilson sexually abused boys in his care over decades from 1971 to 1996 while at Dilworth.

He was first convicted in 1997 on a charge relating to the abuse, and ordered to pay a fine. He was also given name suppression.

A previous Parole Board decision said Wilson represented himself to the court as "a first offender without any other offending," and did not disclose his significant other cases of abuse at the time.

But Wilson had sexually abused other boys.

He was convicted again in 2021 on seven charges relating to offending between 1975 and 1992, and sentenced to three years and seven months behind bars.

When the Parole Board asked him if there were more victims who were yet to come forward, Wilson said he was not aware of any.

But in 2023, further victims came forward and Wilson was convicted on 19 further charges relating to abuse between 1971 and 1992.

There were ten charges of offending against boys under 12, six charges of offending against boys aged 12 to 16, and three charges against a boy over 16. Wilson had a year and 11 months added to his sentence.

He had abused at least 10 different victims, several of them repeatedly over a number of years.

The Dilworth Trust Board has earlier apologised and acknowledged decades of sexual and physical abuse at the school.

Wilson was arrested in 2020 as part of Operation Beverly - the police investigation into historic sexual offending at Dilworth.

Police have made 14 arrests as part of the operation. Seven people have been convicted. Three others died before their cases could be heard in court.

Wilson had been denied parole at his previous six board hearings.

Harding had also attended each hearing. He told RNZ that he is asked why he attended the hearings.

World.title: AFL wildcard matches and times confirmed
World.content:
Carlton are confident they can "do some damage" in the AFL finals from 10th spot as they eye a wildcard round clash with Melbourne.

Josh Fraser's men will take on the Demons on Saturday night at the MCG in the second of two knockout wildcard clashes next weekend under the new format.

The Western Bulldogs will meet Collingwood in the first wildcard match on Friday night, also at the MCG.

AFL wildcard matches, dates and times Western Bulldogs [8th] vs Collingwood [9th]: Friday, August 28, 7:40pm AEST, Melbourne Cricket Ground Melbourne [7th] vs Carlton [10th]: Saturday, August 29, 7:35pm AEST, Melbourne Cricket Ground

If Melbourne win, they will travel to Adelaide while the winner out of Western Bulldogs and Collingwood will visit Geelong.

If Carlton win, they will travel to Geelong while the winner of the other wildcard match will play away to Adelaide.

Carlton are the hottest team in the lower finals bracket after a comprehensive win over ladder leaders Fremantle in round 24 on Saturday.

It extended their unbeaten streak to five matches, with 11 wins and a draw in 14 outings since Fraser took the coaching reins in May.

Carlton previously sneaked into the finals from ninth when arch-rivals Essendon were banished from the 2013 campaign as punishment over the supplements scandal.

The Blues were knocked out in week two that year but appear capable of making a deep finals run this time from the platform of the league's first wildcard round.

"You need to show up and if you play the right way then I feel like you can do some damage," Blues forward Brodie Kemp told AAP.

"We've got some momentum going into wildcard and [beating Fremantle] was a great way to do it.

"Wins on the board means that you've got evidence that you can play a good brand and it stacks up against good sides."

Initially appointed on an interim basis after Michael Voss was sacked, Fraser secured the job as full-time coach when he engineered one of the great in-season turnarounds to steer Carlton to a wildcard spot.

Kemp said the 44-year-old had put a greater emphasis on skills during the week to add another dimension to the Blues' game style, which is reaping rewards.

"We always had that contest and stoppage game with Vossy, and he did a lot of work on the foundations of our game," Kemp said.

"[Now we have] the ability to possess the ball a bit more while nailing the fundamentals, and that's probably the biggest shift for us.

"We're playing for each other and it's really fun to be a part of … but finals-type heat adds a different layer.

"It's not going to go all our way the whole time, so we need to adapt and stay connected and we're in a really good position to be able to do that."

Carlton expect to welcome back Will Hayward and Nick Haynes from ankle injuries against Melbourne, who are monitoring fresh knee problems for Matt Jefferson and Dan Turner.

The Bulldogs could be without spearhead Aaron Naughton (ankle) for their meeting with Collingwood, who have lost veteran Scott Pendlebury and Brayden Maynard to knee issues.

Dogs ruckman Tim English (knee) is an outside chance to return.

AAP

World.title: Australia's bowling attack can't disguise batting failings forever
World.content:
It would be very easy to look at the bare numbers of Australia's two-day, innings victory over Bangladesh in Mackay and see them as a sign that normal service has resumed.

The number-one-ranked Test side has flexed its muscles on home soil and pounded the tourists into the dust.

Same old Australia, always winning. Nothing to see here.

But to think this victory has covered over the fault lines exposed by a disastrous defeat in Darwin a week ago would be to bury one's head in the sand.

The catastrophic issues that resulted in a stunning defeat a week ago have not disappeared.

Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

It is just that in Mackay, Australia's four galloping horsemen of the Apocalypse rode to the rescue, aided by a friendly pitch, albeit one far less treacherous than the batting card would have us believe.

"I don't think it should necessarily have been a two-day game," Josh Hazlewood said after the match to Fox Sports.

"I think there was obviously a little bit of seam movement day one in the morning … You'd expect that in most Test matches.

"But once the shine went off the ball it didn't do a great deal from a bowling point of view."

Yet just 369 runs were scored for the loss of 30 wickets in two days of play, an average of 11.2 runs per batter.

Mitchell Starc claimed 10 wickets across the match for the fourth time in his Test career. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Mitch Starc will get the headlines and so he should; his 10-51 is evidence that at 36 he is still more than capable of beguiling a team with his mastery of left-arm seam bowling.

The devastation he wrought on the hapless Bangladeshi batters was total, a cyclonic burst of relentless energy a Mackay weather watcher would have found familiar.

His first-inning spell of 5-5 on that opening morning, his five wickets coming in a thrilling 22-ball burst that started from the very first delivery of the match, was of a force-of-nature quality that simply cannot be withstood.

Bangladesh's batters, so disciplined and patient in Darwin, walked into an ambush armed only with matchsticks for all the use their bats were against such terrifying pace and accuracy.

Starc claimed four ducks, two of them golden, during that sparkling spell, then followed up by taking three wickets in two overs to start the second innings.

Of the 10 batters Starc accounted for in the match, six fell without scoring.

And when he tired, it was up to Pat Cummins, who took three wickets in each innings, with Nathan Lyon chipping in with three of his own on the second day of another rapid-fire Test that only required two days to complete.

Pat Cummins took six wickets in the match, three in each innings. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This was the third Test only lasting two days of the past seven played on Australian soil.

In fact, four of the past 20 Tests in Australia have been financially ruinous — done and dusted before doors could open on a third day.

And so much of that comes down to the firepower inherent in that battery of bowlers, a line-up containing four of the top 12-ranked bowlers in Test cricket. Australia has enough quality to leave the player ranked sixth by the ICC, Scott Boland, kicking his heels on the bench.

They went to town on a Gabba-like pitch that offered seam and bounce more to their liking than the low and slow Darwin deck.

But what of the batters?

Opener Matt Renshaw made just eight runs. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

After Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins had blown Bangladesh away for 64 before tea on day one, the stage was set for the under-pressure batters to cash in and go big, proving their worth ahead of a trip to a South Africa that is likely to be far from hospitable.

Only four managed double figures — and one of those was Nathan Lyon.

Matt Renshaw made eight, the increasingly under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne four and Alex Carey a paltry five as once more the house of cards came tumbling down at the slightest breath of wind.

Take nothing away from Shoriful Islam, whose 7-48 were career-best figures in Test cricket.

Shoriful Islam went on a tear for Bangladesh. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

But aside from a miraculous inswinging yorker to dismiss Cameron Green on the morning of day two, the other batters were too easily removed.

"I think our bowling has got us out of trouble a lot in Test cricket over the last four or five years," former Australia skipper Alyssa Healy said on Fox Sports's commentary.

"We had a really good run with Marnus in form, Steve in form, Travis in form at different points in time, but the bowling has been really consistent.

"While they're consistent … then you can make the changes in the batting line-up and get them settled.

" We're not going to be blessed with this bowling attack for very long. "

Australia's collapse from 4-145 to 8-148 means a rejigging of the middle order has to be considered.

Head has scored more runs than anyone for Australia as a makeshift opener, but his method of dismissal, playing on with an angled bat all three times he has been bowled, coupled with the shaky middle order, suggests he needs to return there.

Labuschagne appears so wrought over his lack of form that an extended absence from the Test team may well do him good, although the success of Cameron Green this tour suggests that if Australia stick with him, he may yet return to scoring runs.

Green's 67 was classy and assured amid the chaos, the all-rounder a changed man since that drought-breaking ton in Darwin.

Cameron Green scored another half-ton, the only batter to stand up as others crumbled around him. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Does his poise mean Beau Webster should be dropped for another specialist batter?

As has been discussed, the lack of real quality hammering on the door through the Shield means the list of aspirants is frustratingly short, with so few of the specialist openers in domestic cricket fancied by the selectors.

With no red-ball cricket before the team jets off to South Africa, the selectors are in an unenviable position.

Australia has been limping through Test success off the back of its aging quicks. The moment they are no longer there to provide a rescue, the pressure will really be on.

World.title: Piastri struggles after slow pit stop, Norris wins as Verstappen crashes
World.content:
Reigning world champion Lando Norris has doubled his grand prix win tally in 2026, producing a pair of brilliant overtakes to win the Dutch Grand Prix.

Norris won the last grand prix in Hungary before the mid-year break, and continued that good form while teammate Oscar Piastri struggled for pace.

Mercedes championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who led for stretches in Zandvoort, finished second ahead of teammate George Russell who obeyed team orders in the late stages of the race.

Oscar Piastri was running third, but lost the position thanks to a slow pit stop. The Australian struggled for pace in the second half of the race and finished a distant sixth.

A slow pit stop from McLaren cost Oscar Piastri third place early in the Dutch Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAP Images/Pauline Ballet)

But the day belonged to Norris, who lost the lead on a second restart after the race was red-flagged on the first lap after Max Verstappen lost control of his Red Bull and smashed into the barrier.

"A tough race. I made it tough for myself, but a good race, well fought," Norris said.

"Probably one of my better wins. We had to fight for it well, but the pace was very strong.

"I managed things incredibly well today. Over the moon, very, very happy and nice to win the final race here in Zandvoort."

Despite rain falling in the hour before the grand prix, all drivers started on dry tyres, but Verstappen lost control of his Red Bull on a damp part of the circuit and hit the barriers hard.

Norris lost the lead off the restart to Antonelli, with the teenager quicker in the opening laps.

Oscar Piastri, who lost a position at the race start, jumped from fifth into third at the restart and was in contention for a podium.

But the Australian suffered a slow pit stop on lap 18 of 72, dropping him behind Russell. Piastri would struggle for pace for the remainder of the grand prix.

As the race wore on, Norris proved to be quicker in his McLaren as Antonelli struggled with grip. The McLaren came in for his second stop seven laps later than Antonelli, giving him a massive tyre advantage.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton was left out for much longer than his rivals, and was holding the lead of the race as Antonelli and Norris both caught him at the same time.

Norris produced a brilliant move around the outside of Antonelli into the first corner of lap 54, and then passed Hamilton later in the lap to re-take the lead and seal victory.

"The move [on Antonelli] was good, I knew I was not going to get many chances," Norris said.

"Every lap I spent behind him, my odds were getting lower and lower.

"I saw Lewis defending and I knew that was my moment.

"That move won me the race."

Some drivers, including Antonelli, pitted under a late virtual safety car. Antonelli dropped behind Russell, but Mercedes called team orders and the 19-year-old was allowed through.

Russell held on for third with Ferrari duo Hamilton and Charles Leclerc chasing him all the way to the finish line.

Liam Lawson, racing for Red Bull in place of the injured Isack Hadjar, placed seventh, ahead of Audi's Nico Hülkenberg.

With an upgraded car, Fernando Alonso was ninth for Aston Martin, while Pierre Gasly was 10th for Alpine.

Relive all the action of the Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix on the blog below.

World.title: Quick hits: A Shoriful stunner amid more left-arm carnage in the 29th two-day Test
World.content:
Mitchell Starc delivers once more but it's another left-arm seamer who delivers the ball of the series, as Test cricket is blessed with its 29th two-day match.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Shoriful's ball of the series

Cameron Green was felled by a brutal inswinging yorker. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

It wouldn't have taken a rocket scientist to determine that Cam Green held the key for Australia at the start of day two.

The towering all-rounder, buoyed by his drought-breaking ton in Darwin, was once again looking precisely the player he had for so long promised to be.

With Green well set on 67 and clattering boundaries to either side of the wicket, it was going to take something special to remove the big man.

And Shoriful Islam, having already ripped through Australia's middle order late on day two, delivered something very, very special.

The left-armer's pinpoint yorker swung in late and dramatically, with Green falling over himself in a futile attempt to keep it out.

The ball thudded into the Australian's big toe on its way past the stumps and, after a brief consultation with DRS, was given out LBW to what was surely the ball of the series.

And that wasn't the end of the story for left-arm seamers on day two …

2. Starc continues the left-arm carnage

Mitchell Starc picked up from where he left off in the second innings. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Shoriful, who was almost inconceivably yanked from the bowling attack after that stunner against Green, ended the innings with figures of 7-48, the best-ever return for a Bangladeshi bowler while playing away from home.

Combine that with the 6-12 Mitchell Starc plundered early on day one, and left-arm seam had returned overall figures of 13-60, while accounting for 13 of the 20 wickets to fall in the match.

And it wasn't long before those numbers were improved even further.

He couldn't manage a wicket in his first set, but Starc struck with his eighth delivery of the innings, extracting some extra bounce to have Shadman Islam caught off a leading edge at point.

And the very next ball, Starc had his eighth of the match, having kissed the top of Mominul Haque's off stump with the Bangladeshi attempting an ill-advised leave.

An almost-customary double strike from Australia's supreme new-ball destroyer.

Starc eventually finished with figures of 4-39 for the innings and, with 10-51, the second-best match figures of his career.

3. Smith takes a screamer after tea

Tailender Taskin Ahmed had set himself well in the lead-up to the tea break, but he fell at the very first hurdle in the evening session.

Lyon's first delivery was a beauty, pitching and turning away from the leftie, who swung hard and found a healthy outside edge.

And Steve Smith, in place at his familiar position at slip, had to have his wits about him to complete a very good one-handed grab.

He's Test cricket's most prolific catcher for a reason, after all.

Taskin, who had provided perhaps Bangladesh's brightest spot in an otherwise pitch-black innings in swatting a massive six over long on in the shadows of tea, was out for 7.

4. The shortest session ever?

With Shoriful in at No. 11, the end was very clearly nigh in Mackay.

However, Shoriful showed in the first innings that he had at least some ability with the bat, top scoring with a rather frenetic 14 from 19 deliveries.

He survived the first ball of his second dig, defending Lyon out into the off side.

But it was all over with the very next ball.

Shoriful had a big swing at one, caught a thick outside edge and ballooned a dolly out to Starc at point, with Australia's superlative spearhead fittingly bringing the match to an end.

With two wickets falling in just three balls, it had to be close to the shortest non-weather-affected session in Test history.

5. The 29th two-day Test

Australia cruised to victory within two days. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

There have been 2,632 Test matches played in cricket's lengthy red-ball history, with 457 of them held in Australia.

As of today, there have been just 29 finish inside two days.

Only five of those have happened in Australia.

And yet, in the last 20 Tests that have been played on these shores, it has happened four times.

Australia thumped South Africa on a Gabba green top in 2022, and then there were two, two-day Tests during last summer's Ashes, one in Perth and the other at the MCG.

The only Australia-hosted Test to finish inside two days before that game in Brisbane four years ago took place in Melbourne against the West Indies, in February 1931.

Eleven of the two-day Tests in history took place before World War I (between 1882 and 1912), a further three either side of World War II (1931-1946) but then none between 1946 and 1999.

Then, since 2000, there have been 13 two-day Tests. The cost of a fast-paced world, perhaps.

World.title: Swans AFLW captain says support 'just unbelievable' as record smashed
World.content:
Sydney AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy wasn't sure what to expect for her side when they ran out for the first instalment of a historic double-header at the SCG.

The Swans dominated headlines across the country all week, filling both front and back pages of every newspaper, for a scandal that called the club's culture into question.

Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal Sydney Swans fans react to an emotional week, where a scandal continues to engulf the club, as they prepare to watch a historic double header at the SCG.

What the women's team got was an outpouring of support which broke the side's attendance record with 16,672 fans filling the stands to watch them play.

That is more than double the previous club record of 8,264.

"It's amazing. We weren't sure what we were going to expect this week, but to see the support that we've received today is just unbelievable," McEvoy told Fox Footy after the game.

"The members and fans are so tight and they know that we're united as a club and we're better than what we were at the start of the week.

The Swans doubled its crowd attendance record. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

"I'm just so grateful to have the support that we had today and the girls were able to turn it on.

"We had a few nervous girls, that's for sure, but we absolutely turned it on."

The scenes were particularly celebratory on the ground post-siren, after Sydney beat Essendon by 24 points.

It was just the second time the women have played on the SCG for premiership points and the first in a double billing with the men's.

Loading Instagram content

Before locking in to warm up, star men's players Errol Gulden and captain Callum Mills got around the women's players.

Gulden was also seen going up to the crowd giving the fans a big thank you for turning out in droves.

Some of those fans left before the men's game, as a boycott had been suggested in the days before the match as a scandal continues to engulf the club.

It's unclear how many fans left in protest to the scandal, but a steady stream was seen leaving.

Swans players spent time with fans after the game. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Swans fans cheer from the stands. (Getty: Darrian Traynor/AFL Photos)

Lulu Clarke, who has been a Sydney Swans fan for as long as she can remember, was one of the fans who walked out.

Ms Clarke had bought a ticket to the men's game, unaware the women were also playing, but once the news broke of the incident she knew she would not be staying for both games.

"Of late, I've definitely drifted apart from the Swans and the AFL industry as a whole," Ms Clarke said.

"I decided that I'm absolutely not going to the men's game, even if those five players were still stood down. There's no way I could just show up and watch it. It just didn't sit right with me."

Former Matilda Sarah Walsh also left the stadium after the women's game, saying it had been a "tough week", but stressed she was not boycotting the men's team.

"It's not a new story but I have a five-year-old daughter who I brought here today to support the women's team," Ms Walsh said.

"I think you can have a club and not expect someone to be a fan of both teams.

"I think that's the nuance of sport, don't expect Socceroos fans to be Matildas fans … We've got a long way to go in society. I don't think this is a Sydney Swans issue at all … it's a societal issue and we all need to do better."

Swans fans Kayley and Georgia went to the SCG to support the AFLW side. (ABC)

Swans fans Kayley and Georgia told ABC News they were there to support the women and will likely just watch a bit of the men's game.

"It's very disappointing from the men's team … I feel like we were very disappointed in everything that happened," Georgia said.

Kayley said the situation was upsetting.

"We've been supporting the Swans since we were kids as well. So, it was just shocking," she said.

"We never thought that any players from this team could do something like this. It was really upsetting."

Many fans held signs during the game along the lines of "I'm here for AFLW".

World.title: Wrong landmark spotted on Sydney Marathon medal a week out from event
World.content:
Runners gearing up for the Sydney Marathon next weekend will receive a medal featuring a football stadium in Germany instead of Moore Park due to an "unfortunate error".

Organisers say the design on the back of the 2026 medal features eight circles to represent the Abbott World Marathon Majors, encircled by a "beautiful Sydney skyline" that "brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way".

However, a structure meant to depict the Sydney Football Stadium, which under naming rights is currently Allianz Stadium, was actually the Allianz Arena in Munich.

Eagle-eyed internet dwellers were quick to recognise the blunder among local landmarks like the harbour bridge, Sydney Tower Eye and St Mary's Cathedral.

The Allianz Arena football stadium in Munich, Germany. (WikiCommons: Tobias Alt)

Sydney Marathon acknowledged the issue, saying it was not going to run away from the mistake.

"A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium. We're not going to run from it," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"It was an unfortunate error, though it's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."

The organisers did not apologise and made clear there would not be a replacement medal.

The organisers say the mistake adds "international flavour". (Supplied: Sydney Marathon)

"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive. It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique," they said.

"We're grateful to our participants and partners for taking it in such good humour.

"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget."

Artist distances himself from error

The front of the medal features a blue and white Indigenous design by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian.

In an Instagram story, he said he was not involved in the design for the back of the medal.

"My artwork and creative contribution to this year's medal was specifically for the lanyard and the front side of the medal only," he said.

Ambrose Killian designed the front of the 2026 Sydney Marathon medal. (Supplied: Sydney Marathon)

"I had no involvement in the design or production of the reverse side of the medal, including the incorrect inclusion of Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, rather than Allianz Stadium in Sydney.

" I take my work very seriously and would like to reiterate that my artwork story, importance and originality remains. "

This year's Sydney Marathon has set a record participation with 40,000 entrants stepping up to the start line on Sunday, August 30.

The 42.2 kilometre course starts at the North Sydney Oval, before going over the harbour bridge, looping through the city, heading south to Kingsford and snaking back to Centennial Park, with participants crossing the finish line at the Sydney Opera House.

World.title: Tigers score upset of the NRL season with 79th-minute winner
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have slipped on a Wests Tigers-shaped banana skin in a shock 25-24 loss that could prove fatal in their pursuit of the NRL's minor premiership.

Halfback Jock Madden was the hero for the Tigers on Sunday, kicking a 79th-minute field goal to snap a eight-game losing run.

The Tigers' finals hopes ended months ago and they were ranked $10 outsiders at the Sydney Football Stadium.

But led by co-captain Api Koroisau, Benji Marshall's side produced one of the upsets of the season to turn the make-up of the top four on its head.

With two rounds remaining, the Roosters (38 points, +162) sit third after blowing a golden chance to move clear of the ladder-leading Warriors (38 points, +295) and second-placed Penrith (38 points, +294).

"It was a poor game from us," said Roosters coach Trent Robinson, adding the result "wasn't good" for his side's top two hopes.

"There's two games to go and it's pretty clear.

"In the end we didn't win today and the ladder is where it's at and we know what we want to do.

"We still want to be the best team in the comp this year and the opportunity is still sitting right there."

The best win of Benji Marshall's tenure has thrown the NRL's top four into chaos. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

In further bad news for Robinson, lock Victor Radley was placed on report and underwent a late head injury assessment.

The Roosters coach was unsure post-match if Radley had passed his concussion test.

Wests Tigers had every reason to not aim up on Sunday, especially when prop Alex Twal was ruled out with a head knock inside 60 seconds and Roosters winger Billy Smith touched down after just three minutes.

But unlike the past few months when they would have gone to water, the Tigers stood up for themselves.

"I reckon that's as proud as I've ever been as a coach, given we lost Twaly who is probably our most experienced player," Marshall said.

"We had guys, without sugar-coating it, who were on development deals playing against the team that was coming first.

"I'm just proud, proud of the effort, and I'd probably go as far as saying that as a club that's probably one of our best wins we've had."

Smith's opener sparked the Tigers into life with Patrick Herbert setting up winger Jeral Skelton for two tries and back-rower Tony Sukkar for one inside 26 minutes.

Madden's inability to nail any of the three conversions meant Sam Walker was able to tie the game up at 12-12 at halftime when he converted Smith's second.

Tries to Solomone Saukuru and Koroisau, who took charge of the goalkicking and booted a 40/20, pushed the Tigers further ahead.

Robert Toia crashed over for the home side but Walker rattled the conversion into the left upright, giving the Tigers 15 minutes to defend an eight-point lead.

The Roosters looked to have finally found their mojo after Mark Nawaqanitawase had a try chalked off before setting up Walker with a brilliant offload that cut the deficit to two.

After Hugo Savala was tackled off the ball, Walker made it 24-24 with a penalty goal with less than five minutes remaining.

A blunder from Roosters prop Naufahu Whyte put the Tigers back on the attack and when Radley was ordered off for his concussion test, they had time to get in position for a field-goal attempt.

Madden, who has missed the past month after a haematoma in his nether regions, calmly delivered.

"It was quite ballsy for him to play today," Marshall said with a wink.

"I'm really proud. Under pressure, to kick that to win the game was awesome."

Cronulla did just enough to beat the Titans. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam )

Earlier, Cronulla snapped a shocking two-game losing streak to revive their NRL top-four finals hopes with a potentially season-saving 30-22 win over the lowly Gold Coast.

The victory was anything but convincing as the Sharks recovered from an eight-point second-half deficit to prevail at Skilled Park on Sunday.

Quietening some doubters, Cronulla will nevertheless bank the priceless two competition points and move on after staying in the hunt for an all-important double chance in the looming finals.

No team in NRL history has won the premiership from outside the top four.

AAP

World.title: 'Mainly to support AFLW': Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal
World.content:
Sydney Swans supporter Teri turned up to the SCG with a homemade sign reading: "I'm here for the AFLW".

"[I'm here] mainly to support AFLW women in light of everything that's happened. They still need our support," Teri said.

"I still love the game and I still love Sydney, just extremely disappointed."

Sydney Swans play after Pullman Hotel scandal Sydney's AFLW team takes the field in the first game of a double-header, with some fans threatening to walk out on the following men's game. Follow live.

She is one of many fans who have descended on the SCG ahead of the historic double-header between the men's and women's teams. It comes in an emotional week as a scandal continues to engulf the club.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Swans fans arrive at the SCG ahead of the historic double-header. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Teri, a decades-long supporter of the club, expressed great disappointment.

"As a fan, as a decades supporter, always thinking this club was something better, raising up against racism, like back to Goodsey … I thought they were much better than this," she said.

"It's hard to be proud at the moment."

She said she would play it by ear whether she stays for the men's game.

"It's got nothing to do with the women, and I think they are suffering as well … these are people they thought were their friends," Teri said.

"It was important for me to make sure that I came out for the women, wear my women's AFLW merch, so that's the first thing and I'll decide as I'm there because I also feel for the remainder of the team, the men's team."

There was talk during the week of a fan boycott of the men's game, where some fans have decided to show up for the AFLW game between Sydney and Essendon and leave before the men's Swans team run out against North Melbourne.

Swans spectators arrive for the AFLW match between Sydney Swans and Essendon Bombers at the SCG. (Gett6y: Cameron Spencer)

For long-term fan and member Meagan Masters, the past week has left her "gutted", saying the image of the "wholesome" club had been shattered.

"I feel like I know the players, and so just disappointment and really heartbroken for the other members of the team at this stage in the competition where they were heading possibly to a flag," she told the ABC as she made her way to the SCG.

She said the alleged actions of the five players was "unacceptable" for professional athletes, and she was "100 per cent" behind their ban for the remainder of the season, but said she was keeping an open mind because no-one knows exactly what happened at the hotel.

Meagan Masters says this week has left her "gutted" and "heartbroken". (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

Ms Masters, who regularly goes to both the men's and women's games, said she expected a large turnout today.

"I think we're going to get that record crowd that we're after," she said.

" I love the girls, I love the boys and I think they're still going to be banded as a club. Just five guys doesn't define a club. The Swans are more than that. "

Fans grapple with Swans scandal Sydney Swans fans are grappling with an emotional week of developments ahead of a historic double-header, as a scandal continues to engulf the team.

David Lipman also there to support the women's team, agreed that fans would turn out in droves.

"They've [women's team] done nothing wrong," he said.

"They may feel that what's alleged to have occurred is detrimental to their standing, but the rest of the club are supporting them and they deserve it."

Swans fans queue up to enter ahead of Sydney's AFLW match against Essendon. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Chris Lewis goes to most AFLW games in New South Wales and came out in a GWS pride kit to support the AFLW game today.

"[I'm feeling] incredibly disappointed. There is no doubt about that it's been probably the worst week for NSW footy that we have ever had," he said.

"It's been horrible, it's been horrible as a parent to young kids, trying to explain this stuff when they were fans of some of the players involved. It's just been an absolute awful week for all footy fans in NSW."

Chris Lewis came out to support the Sydney Swans AFLW side at the SCG. (702 ABC Sydney: Georgie Carroll)

On whether he would stay for the men's match, similar to Teri he said he would play it by ear, but likely would not stay.

"I've been trying to weigh this up all week. I'm a big fan of the North Melbourne men's team, especially Cooper Trembath, but I'll probably be leaving. It just doesn't seem appropriate, it doesn't seem right to stay," he said.

Tech.title: GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series
Tech.content:
It’s been over a decade and two console generations since GTA V came out, and its sequel is still a work in progress. GTA VI has faced multiple delays, with developer Rockstar Games bumping back its predicted release date twice, first to May 26th, 2026, then again to November 19th, 2026, a full year after its originally planned release window of fall 2025, and facing accusations of union busting after firing more than 30 employees.

Early official glimpses offered a look at the game’s protagonists, Jason and Lucia, as the game will follow the pair around Vice City as they attempt to navigate a criminal conspiracy after a job goes south. After leaks of early builds a few years ago, a new “CyberLeek” series of posts have popped up, showing sequences of the game just days ahead of Rockstar’s planned Netflix-exclusive (for six hours) event on August 27th.

Tech.title: We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is an intimate coming-of-age horror film
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Jane Schoenbrun’s latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, is making a splash in theaters right now. So it seems like the perfect time to revisit their first film, We’re All Going to the World’s Fair. I fell in love with this film when I first saw it at Sundance in 2021.

We are immediately introduced to our protagonist, Casey, as she engages in the World’s Fair Challenge, a sort of ARG creepypasta meets ice bucket challenge. There’s a creepy mantra, some bloodletting, and a mysterious video — basically a speedrun of horror movie tropes. But having them all delivered by this young girl alone in her room who just stares directly into her webcam the whole time is unsettling. And I actually physically recoiled when she jabbed herself repeatedly with a pin to draw blood.

The idea is that people perform the ritual and then they’re supposed to change in some sort of nebulous way. It’s set up as some sort of “game” where people are supposed to report their symptoms, as they turn into plastic or their guts and become Tetris pieces.

Ultimately, World’s Fair is a coming-of-age story about a lonely young girl. She’s never shown talking to kids her own age. Her father is never seen, only heard, and does nothing but yell. She desperately attempts to connect with others by uploading videos documenting the changes she experiences after performing the challenge.

Importantly, unlike many other coming-of-age films, World’s Fair isn’t about Casey’s sexual awakening and avoids sexualizing her entirely. Instead, it’s about her search for belonging in an extremely online world.

Basically the only other character to get any screen time is JLB, a lonely middle-aged man who claims Casey is in danger. The relationship between JLB and Casey adds another layer of unease to the film, which already blends horror elements with uncomfortably intimate glimpses into the life of a young girl. The whole thing has a voyeuristic quality. It’s never explicitly stated, but it certainly seems like JLB is attempting to groom the vulnerable Casey.

The movie stews in its uncomfortable ambiguity. And that’s part of what makes it great. It may not reach the surreal or campy heights of I Saw the TV Glow or Camp Miasma, but it’s a rare indie cinema original that uses body horror tropes in new and interesting ways.

We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is available to stream on Criterion Channel, Kanopy, and Hoopla.

Tech.title: Grand Theft Auto VI exists in its own universe
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on GTA VI and the state of the video game industry, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Four years ago, fans got a long-awaited look at Grand Theft Auto VI with a huge cache of videos that showed off Rockstar’s latest open-world epic. There were 90 videos in total, providing a glimpse at the next-generation take on Vice City, introducing the game’s new dual protagonists, and generally showing off the crime-fueled mayhem the series is known for. The twist? This wasn’t some official reveal. The videos were part of a massive leak in September 2022 that ultimately ended with a life sentence in a secure hospital for the hacker, and they dropped months before Rockstar properly unveiled GTA VI to the world with its debut trailer.

For many video game studios, a leak of that magnitude would be devastating. But not Rockstar: Following the unprecedented success of GTA V, which has sold more than 230 million copies across PC and three generations of consoles, it seems like there is little that can impact the studio in the lead-up to the sequel’s much-hyped launch. GTA VI’s first trailer was leaked less than a day before it was set to premiere in December 2023, and yet the official video went on to garner nearly 290 million views on YouTube.

How it’s going

The lead-up to the Netflix premiere hasn’t exactly been smooth. Over the last week further leaks have spread unofficial gameplay clips across platforms like Discord and X, and Rockstar has flexed its legal muscles, subpoenaing both Microsoft and Discord in hopes of finding the culprit. This had led to some frustration internally, and potentially changes to how Rockstar approaches security, according to a Bloomberg report. But, once again, it doesn’t seem to have put a dent in the fervor around the game. GTA VI is so big that even small updates, like a cover art reveal, rack up millions of views. And this has allowed Rockstar to do things no one else can. It can reveal gameplay through a mainstream platform like Netflix, and maintain sustained interest in the game despite only releasing two trailers over the span of several years.

“Grand Theft Auto reveals have become cultural moments in their own right,” Netflix exec Brandon Riegg said when announcing the gameplay reveal. “The anticipation and fandom around Grand Theft Auto VI is unprecedented, and we’re honored that Rockstar Games has partnered with us to debut the next part of the Grand Theft Auto story with Netflix members first.”

This mentality isn’t entirely new for Rockstar, but the success of GTA V has allowed the studio to be more confident with how it reveals and launches games, eschewing the traditional news cycle in favor of, well, whatever it wants. Back in 2016, on a random Sunday afternoon, the studio released an image that was simply its logo on a red background. The internet promptly went into a craze, correctly surmising that Rockstar was teasing the next Red Dead Redemption, an open-world Western series that had been dormant for several years. That game, Red Dead Redemption 2, went on to sell nearly 90 million copies, giving Rockstar another blockbuster to fill the gap between GTAs.

Open-world games have become widespread over the last decade or so, but there’s still no developer that renders its virtual worlds with the level of detail and realism that Rockstar does. That’s true whether we’re talking about a fictional version of modern California or the Wild West at the turn of the century. It’s also probably why the studio can get away with taking so long with GTA VI; fans have been given plenty of reason to believe that it’ll be worth the wait.

And that’s why the steady stream of leaks has done little to diminish the hype around the game. In fact, they’re almost serving as a form of marketing; Rockstar may be content with a drip feed of news and details, but anxious fans are eager to soak up every new detail about the game, whether it’s official or not.

What happens next

GTA VI isn’t a fix for everything ailing the industry, and most of its benefits will be temporary for everyone but Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive. There are also still plenty of questions ahead of its release, like what the future for the enduring multiplayer spinoff GTA Online looks like, or whether GTA VI’s satirical slant on Florida will still feel relevant after such a long development cycle. But for at least a few weeks later this year, players can pretend everything is normal while they lay waste to Vice City once again.
